10022-white-queen-of-the-cannibals-the-s:
A. J. Bueltmann's book tells the story of Mary Slessor of Calabar, the Scottish missionary called the White Queen of the Cannibals. Its chapters begin in a drunkard's home, follow a brave girl to Africa, and leave her on her own, into the jungle.

Later chapters show her as a brave nurse, facing witchcraft and the poison test, as she works among the peoples of Calabar. Bueltmann writes for young readers, in an admiring, missionary tone. The book remains a popular life of a remarkable woman, whose courage and kindness won trust in a dangerous land.
10619-an-englishman-s-travels-in-america:
J. Benwell published An Englishman's Travels in America in 1857 after four years living on the North American continent. He had kept notes of what struck him, not at first for print, and later shaped them into a book on life and manners in the free states and the slave states. The preface stresses that he kept the wording of his notes where he could.

Benwell writes about towns, farms, work, customs, and the sharp divide over slavery, as an outsider watching a young republic. His tone is curious rather than scolding, and his detail is firsthand. Readers get an English visitor's view of America in the tense years just before the Civil War.
11488-the-poetical-works-of-john-dryden-:
George Gilfillan's 1855 first volume pairs a life of John Dryden with his poems and explanatory notes. Dryden was born in August 1631 at Aldwincle in Northamptonshire, a place given under several spellings. His family came from the north, with Drydens still living in a Scottish town where Gilfillan writes.

An ancestor named John moved from Staff-hill to Northamptonshire and gained Canons-Ashby by marriage with a daughter of Sir John Cope. Dryden's father was a schoolmaster and a Puritan, honoured, it is said, with the friendship of Erasmus. Notes and a critical dissertation follow the life, setting the poems in their age.
11578-the-poetical-works-of-john-dryden-:
George Gilfillan's second volume of Dryden's poetical works, dated 1855, opens with a critical estimate of the poet's genius. Gilfillan asks how far a poet should be tried by the morals and taste of his own age, and warns against judging a former century by nineteenth-century rules or by Scripture alone.

Taste, he argues, is as age-bound as dress: to judge old verse by new fashion is unjust. Later pages weigh Dryden's moral tendency, his varied fruits, and the elements of his genius, with notes explaining the poems. The volume gives a Victorian critic's full case for Dryden, faults and strengths together.
11900-elizabeth-visits-america:
Elinor Glyn's 1909 novel Elizabeth Visits America follows her heroine, the Marchioness of Valmond, from Heaviland Manor and Tonnerre through Cannes and aboard the Lusitania to New York. Contents list the Plaza Hotel, Speistville, and Latour Court on Long Island, mapping a society novel across two continents.

Elizabeth observes American houses with a sharp eye, describing Fifth Avenue rooms of appalling taste, gilding, dreadful Louis XV furniture. Gorged cupids on cannon-ball clouds, beside a good picture or a bit of china. She also admires American go, a mental alertness and lucidity, and notes how Paris hats two feet across become a yard wide in America, yet soon look natural.
12022-a-start-in-life-a-journey-across-a:
C. F. Dowsett's one-shilling book A Start in Life, subtitled A Journey Across America and Fruit Farming in California, was published in London by Dowsett and Company of Lincoln's Inn Fields. It promoted land at Merced, California, with plans, maps, views, books, and samples of fruits and soils on view at the firm's offices.

Dowsett, author of Striking Events in Irish History, writes for emigrants and investors weighing a new life: a journey across America, then the practical business of fruit farming in a new state. The book is both travel account and prospectus, showing how Victorian emigration literature mixed advice, advertisement, and hope in a single cheap volume.
12091-the-camp-fire-girls-at-long-lake-o:
Stewart's Camp Fire Girls at Long Lake, or Bessie King in Summer Camp, was published by Saalfield in Chicago, Akron, and New York in 1914. It is volume 3 of the Camp Fire Girls series. An illustration shows Dolly bound to a tree, a handkerchief over her mouth, hinting at the summer-camp mischief inside.

The first chapter, A Groundless Jealousy, opens with the assurance that the girls are going to be happy at camp. The story follows Bessie King through friendships, rivalries, and campfire ideals. Stewart's series taught girls outdoor skills, loyalty, and service through fiction, in the manner of the Camp Fire movement itself.
12885-bundling-its-origin-progress-and-d:
Henry Reed Stiles published Bundling in 1871 after a quarrel over Connecticut's good name. His history of ancient Windsor had blamed loose camp vices from the old French wars for corrupting New England morals, and sons of Connecticut winced at the charge of a bundling ancestry. Stiles answered with a full investigation of the custom.

Bundling, also called tarrying, let a suitor who had won his hoped-for bride's parents' consent spend one night courting her in bed, both still in undergarments to prevent scandal. If the pair agreed, banns were published and marriage followed fast. If the woman proved pregnant, the man had to marry her or face excommunication, unless he absconded.
13039-shenandoah-a-military-comedy-repre:
Bronson Howard's Shenandoah, a military comedy in the Representative Plays series, is introduced through the playwright's letters to Brander Matthews. The editor praises Howard's noble character, sound mind, gracious manner, and sure grasp of stage craft. The play itself is set at the outbreak of the Civil War.

At a ball, ladies bet bonbons that the United States will not dare fire a shot, and pin ribbons on young heroes. A signal rocket ends the dance, and the men leave partners standing to return to their batteries. Later, a general leaves a rebel girl in a colonel's charge, with a sealed letter as a threat. The comedy mixes romance, loyalty, and war's sudden break into social life.
1375-new-chronicles-of-rebecca:
Kate Douglas Wiggin returns to Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm in new stories of the bright, bookish girl and her life in the Maine village of Riverboro. Rebecca's aunts, her schoolmates, and her dreams of writing all return, with fresh scrapes and small triumphs.

Wiggin writes Rebecca with the same sunny humor that made the first book beloved. The stories are gentle and episodic, full of village color. The book suits readers who loved Rebecca and want more of her growing up. Wiggin's Rebecca stories suit readers who loved the first book.
13757-saracinesca:
F. Marion Crawford set this 1887 novel in Rome in 1865, before the city gained its modern look. Giovanni Saracinesca, heir to an old Roman house, returns to a society of pride, gossip, and strict honour. He loves Corona, a widowed duchess, while family enemies plot against his name and fortune. Duels, debts, and secrets test both lovers.

Crawford paints the Corso, palaces, and salons with close detail. Old Rome, ruled by paternal custom, stands against the coming new order. Giovanni must defend his honour without losing his humanity. Corona matches him in courage and good sense. The novel blends romance, social portrait, and adventure. It remains Crawford's best-known Roman story.
13977-the-argonautica:
Apollonius Rhodius wrote the Argonautica, an epic of Jason and the Argonauts, translated here by R. C. Seaton in 1912. Book one invokes Phoebus, catalogues heroes, and launches the Argo. Jason bids farewell to Alcimede, sacrifices to Apollo, and hears Idmon's prediction. Orpheus sings, Idas boasts, and the ship sails for Lemnos.

Seaton's summary guides readers through Thessaly, Lemnos, and later lands. Augeias, son of Helios and king of the Eleans, joins the crew with hidden armour. The epic blends adventure with Hellenistic learning. Seaton's prose translation suits students and general readers. It remains a standard English Argonautica.
14297-the-congo-and-coasts-of-africa:
Richard Harding Davis, fellow of the Royal Geographical Society, reported the Congo and African coasts for Scribner's in 1907, with his own photographs. Chapters cover coasters, a brother's keeper, the Congo capital, Americans in the Congo, hippo hunting, Old Calabar, and the east coast. Mrs. Davis rides a borrowed hammock while Davis meets wood boys of the Congo.

Coast life supplies vivid detail. Black boys travel second class in open cars, collecting heat and dust over two hundred and fifty miles. Each carries a tin trunk painted pink, green, or yellow, with its key on a knee ribbon. Kroo, Mendi, and Sierra Leone boys never part from their boxes, while a Congo boy owns so little he could carry it in pockets he does not have. Trade rifles, called gas-pipe guns, bear Tower stamps and crowns from Birmingham, flint locks intact. Travel writing, alert and uneasy, from a colonial age.
14627-veronica:
Johanna Spyri, author of Heidi, wrote Veronica and other friends, two stories for children translated from the German by Louise Brooks and published in Boston in 1886. The volume opens with a visit to the doctor.

Veronica grows from a March childhood under blue skies and northern blasts to later trials, with lame Sabina and Mother Gertrude giving good advice along the way. A second tale follows Dietrich and Jost, tempted by a scheme to get rich in one night by cards. Spyri writes with moral warmth about Swiss village life, and the stories suit young readers.
14900-the-black-man-s-place-in-south-afr:
Peter Nielsen's 1922 book asks what place Black South Africans should hold in a country ruled by white men. Nielsen claims the skill of an observer who studied Native ways and thoughts on the spot. He worked at first hand, through their own speech, which he says he knows as well as Natives themselves.

His opening states the question bluntly. The white man, he says, has taken up ruling dark-skinned fellows throughout the world. In South Africa he has carried that task alone, assured of his fitness. Nielsen's answers reflect the segregationist thinking of his time and now read as a document of that era's prejudice. The book is useful as history of ideas, not as a guide to justice.
14970-academica:
James S. Reid, assistant tutor and late fellow of Christ's College, Cambridge, edits Cicero's Academica, the text revised and explained, published by Macmillan in 1874 and dedicated to pupils who read it with him. His preface notes that since Davies in 1725 no English scholar had edited the Academica.

In Germany the last edition with explanatory notes was Goerenz in 1810, whose work Reid calls poor and untrustworthy. Reid therefore offers a new text and notes on Cicero as a student of philosophy and a man of letters. The Academica treats Academic scepticism, knowledge and assent, and Reid's edition remains a scholarly door into Cicero's philosophy for English readers.
15162-scotland-s-mark-on-america:
George Fraser Black's 1921 study, with a foreword by John Foord, traces Scottish influence on America, from colonial emigration to modern industry. Chapters list Scots as governors, signers of the Declaration, presidents, senators, judges, soldiers, sailors, scientists, doctors, and teachers. Literature, church, art, and banking follow.

Black writes as a proud chronicler of a people, not a critic, and his lists run long and detailed. The book serves genealogists and local historians hunting Scottish names in American life. Readers will find it a useful, if celebratory, record of one immigrant group's wide footprint.
15699-a-handbook-of-the-boer-war-with-ge:
A military handbook of the Boer War, issued by Gale and Polden in London and Aldershot in 1910. A general map of South Africa and eighteen sketch maps and plans join the text. The book aims at officers and students who need the campaign in clear order. Its tone is brisk, practical, and proud of British arms.

Chapters open with duty, discipline, and war as a branch of sport, then follow the Natal wedge and the sieges. Kimberley, Ladysmith, and Mafeking each get full treatment, with Baden-Powell at Mafeking. Later chapters press on to Bloemfontein and beyond. As a staff handbook it still gives a compact, map-led view of a hard colonial war.
15958-french-and-english-a-story-of-the-:
A historical tale by Evelyn Everett-Green on the struggle between French and English in America. Five books carry the story: Border Warfare, Roger's Rangers, Disaster, Wolfe, and Within Quebec. Everett-Green, a prolific writer for the young, follows the French and Indian War to its end. The tale mixes invented heroes with real campaigns.

A western settler, friends in need, and Philadelphia open the border war. Robert Rogers and his rangers bring a life of adventure, vengeance, and disaster, with escapes to Albany and Ticonderoga. Wolfe's Louisbourg victory and the impregnable city of Quebec close the arc. The book gives young readers the war for Canada in stirring, readable form.
16399-a-winter-tour-in-south-africa:
Sir Frederick Young recounts a winter tour across South Africa in this 1890 volume, reprinted from the Royal Colonial Institute proceedings with added chapters, pictures, and a map. The voyage runs from Southampton by Lisbon, Madeira, and St. Helena to Cape Town, then on to Kimberley and its diamond mines, with towns, troops, and museums along the way.

Young writes as a proud imperial traveler, keen on the colonies' growth and their sights. The dedication to Princess Louise sets the loyal tone. For readers of Victorian travel, the book gives a full, confident tour of South Africa just before the Boer War changed it forever.
17417-what-prohibition-has-done-to-ameri:
Fabian Franklin published this attack on Prohibition in New York in 1922 with Harcourt, Brace and Company. His chapters argue in order: perverting the constitution, creating a nation of lawbreakers, destroying the federal system, and showing how the amendment was put through. The law makers and the law, the law enforcers and the law, and the nature of prohibitionist tyranny follow.

Later chapters weigh one-half of one percent, prohibition and liberty, and prohibition and socialism, among other charges. Readers get a fierce, early critique of the noble experiment, written while it was still new. Franklin's book remains a clear statement of the case against Prohibition from a constitutional point of view.
17877-south-america:
W. H. Koebel wrote this 1913 history of South America for the Making of the Nations series, published in London by Adam and Charles Black with maps and photographs. Koebel had already written on modern Argentina and Chile, and here he steps back to tell the whole south half of the continent.

Chapters run from the land before Spain came, through Columbus, the conquest of Peru, the early days of Brazil, and the rule of Spain's colonies, to raids by foreign foes. Koebel writes in a plain, school-book style, keen on governors, fleets, and trade. The book gives a clear, if old-fashioned, first survey of South American history for a general reader.
20483-artillery-through-the-ages-a-short:
Artillery Through the Ages gives a short illustrated history of cannon. It was made to help visitors at America's historic sites understand the guns they saw. Photographs show early nineteenth-century field guns and Civil War garrison pieces in place.

The captions name the shrines where the guns stand. Fort Pulaski keeps Civil War garrison guns, while Gettysburg holds field guns from the same war. Petersburg's park preserves its own batteries. The book traces cannon from crude early tubes to rifled artillery, tying each step to battlefields a reader can still walk.
20747-deaconesses-in-europe-and-their-le:
What place should women's church work hold? Deaconesses in Europe asks that hard question head on. The book asks what the early and medieval churches can teach on the point. It also asks if sisterhoods can grow without the harms of convent life.

European deaconess houses, where women served the sick and poor, fill the study. The author weighs their record and asks what America might safely copy. Church history, charity work, and women's roles meet in one debate. Readers get a clear window on a live church question of the late nineteenth century, argued with care.
21059-the-adventures-of-dick-maitland-a-:
Harry Collingwood sends a young doctor's apprentice from London's poor East End into unknown Africa in this adventure novel. Dick Maitland works for a kind doctor who treats the poor for almost nothing. When Dick's family fortunes fall, he works his passage to South Africa with no money at all.

On the ship Dick befriends a rich young man named Grosvenor, and the two set out to explore together. They meet peoples Collingwood had used in an earlier book, then seek a rumoured mysterious white race. Those people prove to be a lost tribe, and Dick returns home with valuable jewels.
21276-the-wars-between-england-and-ameri:
T. C. Smith, professor of American history at Williams College, published this short history in London in 1914. Twelve chapters run from the elements of antagonism in 1763 to the War of 1812 and a closing chapter on a century of peace. Parliamentary taxation, the disruption of the empire, and French intervention mark the first war.

Smith then follows the making of the United States, two periods of trade quarrels, and the war for sailors' rights and westward expansion. A bibliography and index close the book. Written on the eve of the First World War, it reads the old quarrels as a finished story between two now-friendly peoples.
21543-french-pathfinders-in-north-americ:
William Henry Johnson tells of France's explorers in French Pathfinders in North America, copyrighted in 1905. Jacques Cartier's portrait fronts the book, and seven full-page plates fill it. Johnson had already written on the world's discoverers and on pioneer Spaniards.

Early chapters treat the origins of the peoples called Indians and the Iroquois League. Then come Cartier in Canada, Ribaut at Port Royal, and Laudonnière on the St John's River. Champlain's work on the St Lawrence and the Great Lakes takes two chapters. Jesuit mission pioneers and later travellers carry the tale toward the French and Indian War.
21555-the-mission-or-scenes-in-africa:
An autumn expedition in 1828 opens Captain Marryat's The Mission, or Scenes in Africa, published in 1845. An elderly, infirm gentleman leads the party into the interior. One figure had made a fortune in India before ill health drove him home for a spell.

Marryat, who knew Africa from his own service, builds the tale on travel and mission work. Hunting, tribal politics, and the hardships of the road fill the scenes. The book was his twenty-second, late in a run of twenty-six. Its South African ground gives it a flavour unlike his sea tales, with the same gift for episode.
2157-female-suffrage-a-letter-to-the-chr:
Susan Fenimore Cooper, daughter of James Fenimore Cooper, writes in 1870 to Christian women of America on female suffrage, in a two-part magazine article for Harper's New Weekly Magazine. She argues from faith and home life. Cooper wrote in 1870, when suffrage was new and fiercely debated in America.

Cooper asks whether the vote would serve women, families, and the nation, and she answers with caution rooted in Christian duty. The letter gives a clear view of conservative argument in the early suffrage debate, and of one thoughtful woman's mind. Her Christian argument appealed to women who feared the vote would harm home and faith.
21682-the-field-and-garden-vegetables-of:
Fearing Burr Junior describes near eleven hundred vegetables in The Field and Garden Vegetables of America, issued at Boston in 1863. The full title promises each kind's size, form, colour, quality, and season. Hardiness, yield, and value for cultivation are set out for each.

Before Burr, such knowledge lay scattered in fragmentary sources, hard for beginners to find. His book gives directions for propagation, culture, and use in one place. Albert Fearing of Hingham, a backer of farming causes, receives the dedication. For gardeners and seed historians, the volume remains a rich record of American varieties before the modern seed trade.
21699-the-rover-of-the-andes-a-tale-of-a:
R. M. Ballantyne crosses South America in The Rover of the Andes, at about the latitude of Buenos Aires. A journey over the continent's heart carries the reader from chapter to chapter. Nasty folk and nasty happenings block the road, one by one overcome.

Ballantyne researched his settings by living among the men he wrote of, for weeks and months. Telegraph cables, lightships, lifeboats, and divers all drew that treatment from him. The Andes tale feels realistic, its editors say, though built of research and imagination. It carries the reader, panting for the next turn, right to the last chapter.
21766-ionica:
William Cory, born William Johnson in Devon in 1823, published the first Ionica in 1858, a slim green volume of forty-eight poems. A second set followed privately in 1877, printed without stops on the author's odd theory that spaces should mark the pauses. In 1891 he gathered most of both books, with new pieces, into the Ionica known today: eighty-five poems in all.

Arthur C. Benson adds a life of the poet and notes in this edition. Cory had been a master at Eton, and his lyrics carry a schoolmaster's love of Greek and Latin verse. The poems are brief, clear, and tender, often turned toward friendship, loss, and the shortness of life. Ionica became a quiet classic of Victorian lyric poetry.
22323-impressions-of-south-africa:
Impressions of South Africa records a close look at a troubled country in the 1890s. Its author wrote as political problems there grew acute. The closing chapter, written with events of early 1896 in view, still hoped for peace.

The writer believed those problems would be solved in a peaceable way. The qualities needed, he said, were tact, coolness, and patience. Patience, above all, was his repeated plea. That hope gives the book its value now. It shows how a thoughtful observer read South Africa just before war came. Readers can test his judgment against everything that followed in that decade.
22476-the-tale-of-mr-peter-brown-chelsea:
V. Sackville-West wrote The Tale of Mr. Peter Brown, Chelsea Justice, for the New Decameron. Her narrator reproaches himself for a small social failure. A smile, he reflects, would have sufficed in the moment.

The smallest response would have encouraged the other man to speak. Why, the narrator asks, had he not given it? A smile is not much to demand between human beings. He finds it pitiable that convention persuades us to withhold it. A fellow creature, perhaps in need, was refused that trifle. The tale builds its moral weight from that tiny chill. Readers get Sackville-West's fine, quiet prose on manners and regret.
22483-across-unknown-south-america:
Across Unknown South America records an expedition into little-known country. Its opening exchange shows how remote the goal seemed to outsiders. A cinematograph man marvels at the journey's length in amazement.

More than three months to reach the spot, he repeats. Then perhaps Monsieur is on a journey to Mars or the moon! He laughs heartily at his own wit on the spot. No place on earth, he insists, takes so long to reach. The travelers knew better and went anyway into the interior. Their account follows rivers, forests, and peoples rarely visited then. Readers get exploration writing with a camera crew along for the record.
22568-blue-aloes-stories-of-south-africa:
Cynthia Stockley wrote Blue Aloes, stories of South Africa, in 1919. Blue Aloes is a farm whose mistress knows the Karoo well. A night noise frightens a newcomer in the opening story's scene.

It was probably a stray ostrich pecking on your shutters, she says. You are strange to the Karoo, my dear, she adds kindly. When you have been here a month, you will notice nothing. Night noises will stop troubling you by then, she promises. Stockley's stories draw on settler life in dry, wide country. Love, loneliness, and farming hardship run through her South African tales. Readers get a woman writer's view of Karoo farms and folk.
22759-the-english-at-the-north-pole-part:
Jules Verne wrote The English at the North Pole, part one of The Adventures of Captain Hatteras, his novel of Arctic exploration. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Captain Hatteras, an Englishman obsessed with reaching the North Pole, fits out a brig at Liverpool and sails into the ice with a crew that does not know its destination.

The opening quotes the Liverpool Herald of April 1860, noting a brig's departure, an event of little importance for so great a port. Who would notice one vessel among the shipping crowding six miles of docks? Verne builds his epic from that shrug. Hatteras became the type of the polar monomaniac, and the novel, in two parts, is early Verne at full stretch.
23503-in-the-wilds-of-africa:
W. H. G. Kingston wrote this long African adventure of a hero who ships aboard a vessel dogged by misfortune. Officers fall sick, the captain dies, and an unfit officer named Kydd takes charge, until the ship grounds near shore and native attackers slay some of the crew.

Survivors flee on rafts, Kydd on one and the hero with many passengers on another, until a fine vessel picks them up and proves to be a Portuguese slaver. A British warship on slaver patrol attacks, the slaver slips away up a river to a village where it will load slaves, and the heroes go ashore to travel the wilds. Kingston keeps the pace fast and the scenes broad, making a stirring, if period bound, tale of Africa, slavery, and survival.
23643-gudrid-the-fair-a-tale-of-the-disc:
Maurice Hewlett retold a Norse saga in this 1918 novel, centering on Gudrid, daughter of the Icelandic landowner Thorbeorn. Fair, tall, and courteous, she grows up in an Iceland famed for handsome women. Her marriageable years coincide with the westward voyages that carried Norse sailors from Iceland to Greenland and beyond.

Through Gudrid's eyes the reader hears sailors like Biorn describe flat, wooded shores coasted for days, lands passed by and lands settled, and the hard choices of seafaring folk. Hewlett keeps the saga's shape — voyages, kin, and fate — while giving the story the pace and feeling of a modern historical novel.
24165-the-development-of-embroidery-in-a:
Candace Wheeler wrote this illustrated history of American needlework, published by Harper and Brothers in 1921. It opens with the story of the needle. Early chapters cover beginnings in the New World, the crewelwork of Puritan mothers, and samplers and quilts. Later ones treat Moravian work, portraiture, French embroidery and lace, Berlin woolwork, and the revival that founded the Society of Decorative Art.

Later chapters treat American tapestry and the Bayeux tapestries. Pictures show Sioux porcupine quillwork, a colonial crewel tester said to have reached Essex, Massachusetts, in 1640, and a quilted coverlet by Ann Gurnee. Wheeler writes as a maker as well as a historian. Readers get a handsome survey of a craft carried from colonial homes to art.
24297-the-river-of-darkness-or-under-afr:
William Murray Graydon wrote this African adventure novel, copyrighted in 1890 and again in 1902. Its prologue opens in November in London, with the great city buried under a dank, yellow fog and traffic temporizing in the murk. From there the tale runs through stolen despatches, a strange meeting, an Arab's warning, a night on the roof, a fate worse than death, and sale into slavery.

Later chapters bring a separation, a slave prison, Canaris unfolding a tale, a daring move, flight through the town, over the walls, besieged, and the underground river of the title. A journey on the lake, an isle of skeletons, Guy saving Sir Arthur, and Bildad turning cannibal follow. Readers get a breathless Victorian adventure of Africa, above ground and below.
24391-short-sketches-from-oldest-america:
John B. Driggs, M.D., wrote these short sketches from oldest America, published by George W. Jacobs and Company in Philadelphia in July 1905. Its frontispiece shows the Princess and her companion. The publishers' preface notes the immense labor and patient research behind so small a volume. Driggs was first posted to Alaska's northwest in the summer of 1890, and, save two vacations of a year each, stayed constantly at his bleak post ever since.

Landed with his possessions on the beach of the Point Hope peninsula, he sheltered for weeks in a tent of barrels and boxes under canvas. Carpenters from whaling ships raised a house framed in San Francisco, a few hundred yards from the water. A mile away lay a large native village, whose people regarded him as a curiosity, though printed vocabularies and grammars proved inaccurate and valueless. Readers get Alaska's oldest America, sketched at first hand.
24417-the-forest-king-wild-hunter-of-the:
Hervey Keyes copyrighted this tale of the seventeen century, The Forest King, or the Wild Hunter of the Adaca, in 1878. It was printed by Wheat and Cornett on Spruce Street, New York. Its preface opens in the Mohawk valley, a land of flowers where one girl flits through glades. She lifts Mayall's mind to the supernatural, as if to seraph voices. Sweet memory brings him again to life's morning, by his mother's knee and his cradle.

Risen to manhood, Mayall hears the music of the groves and Nelly Gordon's sweet voice, the angel unlocking the harmony of the universe. Her eyes seem pure as morning rays on hills, and her heart expands with thankfulness for all that makes life desirable to Mayall, her lover. Keyes writes this history of Mayall and his family, hunter and trapper of the Adaca valley, from gathered facts. Readers get a Mohawk valley romance.
24591-experiments-upon-magnesia-alba-qui:
Joseph Black, professor of chemistry at Edinburgh from 1766 to 1797, read this paper in June 1755, and it first appeared in print in 1756. The Alembic Club reprinted it at Edinburgh in 1898 as the first of its reprints. Its subject is magnesia alba, quicklime, and other alkaline substances.

Black's experiments uncovered the gas we now call carbon dioxide, and they laid a foundation for modern chemistry. His paper is short, careful, and beautifully reasoned, showing how weighing and testing can reveal what the eye cannot see. Readers of science history will find here a landmark paper, still clear after more than two centuries.
24752-achenwall-s-observations-on-north-:
Gottlieb Achenwall, a professor at Gottingen, published these observations on North America in the Hanoverian Magazine in 1767, from verbal information given by Dr. Franklin. He had visited Germany in the summer of 1766 and met the Gottingen professors. J. G. Rosengarten translated the article, reprinted from the Pennsylvania Magazine of History and Biography in January 1903.

Achenwall's observations describe the British colonies, their people, trade, and government, as Franklin reported them. The piece was reprinted at Frankfort and Leipzig in 1769. The piece is short. It gives a plain report of farms, towns, trade, and laws, in words a general reader can follow. Readers of early American history will find it a fascinating European view of colonial America, on the eve of revolution.
25085-the-stars-and-stripes-vol-1-no-1-f:
The first number of the Stars and Stripes, dated February 8, 1918, is the opening issue of the official newspaper of the American Expeditionary Forces in France. Written by and for American soldiers, it carries a greeting from Commander-in-Chief John J. Pershing, who calls it the soldiers' own paper.

Its pages mix leave rules, warnings against German propaganda, sports, humor, and news from the front, all in the voice of men in uniform. As a historical document it shows how the army spoke to its own troops, building morale, discipline, and a shared identity far from home.
25400-colleges-in-america:
John Marshall Barker's Colleges in America, published in Cleveland in 1894, surveys the growth, functions, and work of American colleges. Barker, with an introduction by Wooster president Sylvester F. Scovel, visited many colleges to gather facts and impressions.

Authorities cited include Painter, Laurie, Boone, Quick, Spencer, Hart, Huxley, Froude, Porter, Tyler, and Thwing. Barker argues that Christian knowledge spurred the search for truth and the training of the race to higher civilized life, and that learning advanced under religion from the Apologists onward. The book dedicates itself to Boston University president William F. Warren.
26180-mother-america:
Sam McClatchie's science-fiction story opens on a football field, where a star runner is hailed as the first Boy America. George Turner tells John Harmon that every university chased the lad, and Harmon notes the boy looks like someone he knows well. The boy is Gloria Manson's son, and his grace on the field hints at more than mere training.

As the tale unfolds, a state-backed plan for planned parenthood takes shape, with a president and Congress giving it official blessing. Gloria grows afraid that she and George are in too deep. The story asks what happens when a nation tries to breed its own heroes, and what such a plan costs the people caught inside it.
27250-what-i-saw-in-america:
G. K. Chesterton's What I Saw in America was published by Hodder and Stoughton in 1922. It opens with his old conviction that travel narrows the mind, unless a man works twice as hard at humility and imagination. Meditations in a New York hotel and on Broadway lead to Irish interviewers, American cities, and the American country.

Chapters take up the business man, presidents and problems, prohibition in fact and fancy, fads and public opinion, and the extraordinary American, whose poetic enthusiasm can be for meat sales themselves. Lincoln and lost causes, Wells and the world state, and the spirits of America and England close a witty travel book.
27852-gold-dust-a-collection-of-golden-c:
Gold Dust, a collection of golden counsels for the sanctification of daily life, was translated and abridged from the French by E. L. E. B. and edited by Charlotte M. Yonge, published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap. The little book gathers short devotional meditations numbered in sequence.

One counsel asks each day for a little work, a little suffering, and a little good to do. Another warns that the first backward step toward sin is almost imperceptible, like snowflakes forming an avalanche. Gentle and practical, the collection belongs to Victorian devotional reading for ordinary days.
28025-the-story-of-john-g-paton-or-thirt:
James Paton retold his brother John G. Paton's life for young readers in this 1892 volume, first issued as a fuller autobiography in January 1889. John Paton was a Scottish missionary who spent thirty years among the peoples of the New Hebrides, now Vanuatu. The book follows him from a plain cottage home in Scotland to the islands.

Chapters cover school days, city mission work in Glasgow, and the long, hard years on Tanna. They include storms, illness, feuds, and the deaths of fellow workers, as well as converts and new schools. Told in plain, earnest prose, the book shows mission life as Paton himself wished young readers to see it.
2857-a-yellow-god-an-idol-of-africa:
H. Rider Haggard's The Yellow God follows Alan Vernon and Barbara into the world of a gold company called Sahara, Limited, and an African idol of the same name. Jeekie, an African servant, tells tales that pull the English characters toward Bonsa town, a hall of the dead, and a gold house where a feast of Little Bonsa is held. Alan falls ill, dreams under the Asika's power, and faces the end of the Mungana.

The novel mixes company fraud in London with ritual power in Africa, as Barbara makes speeches and Mr. Haswell loses his temper. Haggard's adventure keeps its pace through forests, messages, and meetings that decide who lives. It stands as a late Haggard romance about gold, belief, and the price of worshipping wealth.
29083-the-lightning-conductor-discovers-:
C. N. and A. M. Williamson published this travel novel in 1916, told through letters. Patricia Moore, Mrs. Winston, and their friends write home about a motoring tour of America, from Long Island and Easthampton to points further afield. The letters mix scenery, hotels, villages, and the small shocks of English travelers meeting American life.

The Williamsons built the book around the motor car, then still a novelty for long tours, and around the contrasts between old England and a fast-changing America. Readers get an epistolary road story, light and observant, that doubles as a guide to how America looked to friendly foreign eyes just before the First World War reshaped travel.
29223-ponteach-or-the-savages-of-america:
Robert Rogers wrote this play, Ponteach, or The Savages of America, extracted here from Representative Plays by American Dramatists, volume one. Rogers, a soldier of fortune born in New Hampshire, is called the Davy Crockett of colonial times in the volume's introduction. His boyhood on the frontier included withstanding an attack near his home before he turned fifteen.

The play takes its title from Ponteach, the Native leader at its center, and stages the conflicts between Native peoples and colonial settlers. Rogers wrote from a soldier's life on the border. Readers get an early American tragedy of the frontier, rough and ambitious, important for its attempt to put Native history on the colonial stage.
29892-up-the-forked-river-or-adventures-:
Seward D. Lisle, author of Teddy and Towser, wrote Up the Forked River, or Adventures in South America, as number two of the Strange Adventure Series. Henry T. Coates and Company of Philadelphia printed it in 1904, with pictures. A front picture bears the cry I am betrayed, sink the tug, which hints at the perils ahead.

Two friends sit in the private office of Rowland and Starland on Montgomery Street, San Francisco, talking over a subject both love. Each gentleman is past sixty, well preserved, rugged, well to do, and prosperous, with no shadow of difference between them for many years. They toured Europe together and shared many outings. Thomas Starland, the junior partner, reminds his friend Teddy that Teddy reached California years before him. The tale that follows carries them up a forked river.
30162-old-english-patent-medicines-in-am:
George B. Griffenhagen and James Harvey Young trace old English patent medicines in America, in Paper 10 of the Museum of History and Technology series. Bateman's Pectoral Drops, Godfrey's Cordial, Turlington's Balsam of Life, and Hooper's Female Pills head the list, with a half-dozen similar nostrums, mostly English born in the first half of the eighteenth century. Extravagant advertising carried their use swiftly to the American colonies.

Busy settlers with little time and small means took the ready-made, fairly cheap remedies as an answer to scarce medical help. Their popularity bred a host of American imitations and left an impression not soon forgotten. Chapters follow origins, the trip to America, complex formulas and packages, a severed supply, a Philadelphia formulary, the move west, and the medicines in the twentieth century.
30503-the-truth-about-america:
Edward Money, author of works on tea in India and twelve months with the Bashi-Bazouks, offers The Truth About America, published in London in 1886. He opens by noting that Americans and Yankees are not synonyms, and complains of want of courtesy in the States, the press, and a voyage out to New York's climate.

Later chapters follow New York types and currency, a trip to New Orleans, railroads, scenery, ranch life, and deserts in the States. San Francisco, army and navy life, the Pacific coast, and California ranches follow, with Nevada and Utah beyond. Money writes as a frank British traveler, mixing praise, grumbling, and sharp observation.
3066-the-red-man-s-continent-a-chronicle:
Ellsworth Huntington wrote The Red Man's Continent, a chronicle of aboriginal America, for the Chronicles of America series, published by Yale University Press in 1919. Huntington aims first to present the geographical environment of American history in readable form, stressing broad phases of geography that general readers seldom meet. The similarity of form between the Old World and the New is one such phase.

The book describes the Appalachian bands in order, from valley floors flat and fertile to the sharply upstanding crystalline range on the east and the Alleghany plateau escarpment on the west. Huntington links Native cultures to the land that shaped them. The volume now reads as a period work of geography, useful for its maps of environment and its early twentieth-century viewpoint.
30865-my-three-years-in-america:
Count Bernstorff wrote this 1920 memoir of three years in America, in twelve chapters with an index. Its chapters move from Germany and the United States before the war and German propaganda in the United States through political events before the Lusitania incident, economic questions, and so-called German conspiracies. They end with the Lusitania, Arabic, second Lusitania, and Sussex incidents.

Later chapters treat American mediation, the rupture of diplomatic relations, and the return home. Bernstorff opens on his fundamental political views, learned in his father's house at the German Embassy in London. Politics filled the air there, and his father's life was given to the German nation. It is a first-hand diplomatic memoir, valuable for readers of the First World War and of American neutrality.
31110-my-impressions-of-america:
Margot Asquith's 1922 book, published by George H. Doran, records her American lecture tour from her crossing aboard the Carmania to her reflections at large. Chapters follow her arrival in New York, where reporters, hotel splendor, seasickness, and architecture all left marks. They go on to Boston and Worcester, unresponsive Philadelphia, and the White House, where she found President Harding easy to talk to and chatted with Woodrow Wilson.

Later stops take in Detroit and Chicago, with a visit to the Ford works, Pittsburgh and Rochester, Toronto and Montreal, and Ottawa, where she talked with Premier Mackenzie King. Frank, witty, and sometimes tart, the book gives a British visitor's sharp-eyed portrait of America in the early 1920s.
31491-the-baculum-in-the-chipmunks-of-we:
John A. White's The Baculum in the Chipmunks of Western North America was published as University of Kansas Publications, volume five, number thirty-five, pages 611 to 631, with nineteen figures, on December 1, 1953. It studies a small bone in chipmunks. The baculum is a bone found in the reproductive organs of male mammals. It varies in shape between species, and White uses those differences to distinguish chipmunks of western North America, in the genus Eutamias of California and its relatives.

The paper, printed at Lawrence, Kansas, is a technical study for mammalogists, with figures showing each form. Its method is comparative anatomy: measure, draw, and compare, until species separate cleanly. For readers of natural history, it shows how a single small bone can carry taxonomic weight, and how museum specimens turn into species knowledge.
31643-asparagus-its-culture-for-home-use:
F. M. Hexamer's Asparagus, its culture for home use and for market, was published in New York by the Orange Judd Company in 1914. It is a practical treatise on planting, cultivation, harvesting, marketing, and preserving asparagus, with notes on its history and botany. Illustrated throughout, it opens with a picture of the beginning of the asparagus industry in California. Hexamer writes for growers, large and small, who want a crop that pays.

The treatise covers beds, varieties, cutting, bunching, and shipping, with the history of the plant beside its cultivation. For gardeners, it remains a clear, thorough guide to a perennial vegetable. For readers of agricultural history, it records asparagus at the moment it became a commercial crop in America, with California leading the way.
31775-si-klegg-book-5-the-deacon-s-adven:
John McElroy's fifth Si Klegg book, in its second edition of 1912, follows the Deacon's adventures at Chattanooga in caring for the boys. Its twenty-one chapters run from the Deacon provides and a cow in camp through weeks of convalescence, Si's promotion, Shorty in trouble and as orderly, and at last Chattanooga itself.

It begins with the Deacon repaid seventyfold as Si and Shorty relish a stew he cooked for them. They lay wounded in the Chattanooga hospital, to which he had gone as soon as he learned Si was hurt. Readers get a warm, comic volume of the series, where a father's care matters as much as any battle.
31789-the-united-states-and-latin-americ:
John Holladay Latané's 1920 history, published by Doubleday, Page and Company, compares the revolutions of North and Latin America. Latané, professor of American history at Johns Hopkins University, opens with the revolt of the Spanish colonies, contrasting the English colonies' united resistance with the Spanish colonies' spasmodic and disconcerted action.

He argues that the differences are explained not by race psychology alone, but by comparing the English and Spanish colonial systems and the two revolutions themselves. Readers get a scholarly history of how one North American federal republic and many separate Latin American republics grew from different colonial burdens. The book looks at both revolts side by side, not one by one. It asks why one land stayed whole while the lands to the south split apart.
31811-wanderings-in-south-america:
Charles Waterton's Wanderings in South America, in Cassell's National Library edition of 1891 with an introduction by Norman Moore, is the account of an English naturalist. Guiana's forests held him for over a decade. Moore compares Waterton with Gilbert White. White, an Oxford clergyman, never traveled, while Waterton, a Roman Catholic country gentleman educated in a Jesuit college, lived in the north of England and wandered far.

Moore's introduction follows Plutarch's method, setting a Greek and a Roman side by side to show wisdom and imprudence in the same straits. Readers get a classic of natural-history travel, full of Guiana's forests, animals, and adventures, introduced as a life that teaches by example.
31821-so-nnica:
Vicente Blasco Ibáñez's novel Sónnica, translated from Spanish by Frances Douglas and published in New York by Duffield and Company in 1919, is set in ancient Saguntum. Its ten chapters run from At Aphrodite's Temple and Saguntum through dancing girls from Gades, Greek and Celtiberian, invasion, Asbyte and Hannibal, and the walls of Saguntum.

The opening finds the ship of Polyanthus, the Saguntine pilot, returning from Gades and New Carthage, its saffron sail recognized by mariners and fishermen on the breakwater. Meanwhile, the temple of Venus Aphrodite catches the setting sun. Readers get a historical romance of Spain under Rome and Carthage, ending in a hungry city and a last night.
32112-records-of-harvest-mice-reithrodon:
Sydney Anderson and J. Knox Jones, Junior's paper on harvest mice from Central America appeared in the University of Kansas Publications, Museum of Natural History. It was volume 9, number 19, pages 519 to 529, published January 14, 1960. It records harvest mice of the genus Reithrodontomys, with a description of a new subspecies from Nicaragua. The authors write from the University of Kansas at Lawrence.

After Hooper's 1952 review of Latin American harvest mice, Kansas museum collectors visited several Central American countries and gathered many more specimens. Among those specimens, the authors found a new subspecies of Reithrodontomys fulvescens. Readers get a technical faunal paper: locality records, specimen comparisons, and a formal description, useful for mammal distribution rather than for general reading.
3233-in-the-heart-of-africa:
Samuel W Baker's African narrative is condensed here from two larger books. The Nile Tributaries of Abyssinia and The Albert Nyanza, Great Basin of the Nile, supply the matter, cut down by E J W for this volume. The contents open in the Nubian desert, at a bitter well, with a change of plans and an irascible dragoman. Pools of the Atbara and one secret of the Nile follow.

At Cassala the story turns to Egypt's rule of the Soudan, corn-grinding, and the parent of Egypt, the river itself. Baker writes as explorer and hunter together, mapping a river system while shooting his supper. The condensation keeps the journey's spine: desert, river, and lake, with the Nile's mystery drawing the traveler on through heat and hazard.
32331-dave-dawson-at-casablanca:
R. Sidney Bowen's Dave Dawson at Casablanca, in the War Adventure Series, was published by Crown Publishers in New York in 1944 and dedicated to Johnny Bogardus. It follows the air hero of many earlier books. They include Dave Dawson at Dunkirk, with the R.A.F., in Libya, on convoy patrol, at Singapore, and with the Pacific Fleet. They continue with the Air Corps, on the Russian Front, as flight lieutenant, with the commandos, with the Flying Tigers, and on Guadalcanal.

Its chapters run from The Man in Gray and Just in Case through Silent Lips, Orders for Eagles, and Whispering Death. They continue to Changed Orders, Blackout, Eagles Can Take It, Death Strikes, Invisible Eyes, Midnight Raider, and Fighting Hearts. Readers get a Second World War air adventure for boys, where Dave Dawson's squadron war moves to Casablanca, with orders, blackouts, and midnight raids driving the plot.
3236-mr-bonaparte-of-corsica:
John Kendrick Bangs retells the life of Napoleon in this comic history, fifth in a series of his books. The title gives the joke its form: Mister Bonaparte of Corsica, the emperor treated as a neighbor with an address. Bangs follows the boy from Ajaccio through the Revolution's wars to the throne, and then to the long fall.

History here wears a grin. Battles and treaties pass in brisk, joking prose, while Napoleon himself stays human size, ambitious, lucky, and at last unlucky. The joke's form holds throughout: a world conqueror recast as the fellow next door. Bangs never hides the facts, but he refuses to let them stay solemn for long.
32558-sporting-scenes-amongst-the-kaffir:
Captain Alfred W. Drayson's Sporting Scenes amongst the Kaffirs of South Africa, drawn from notes and a rough journal made in the field, describes the Cape country, its people, and its wild animals. Drayson disowns the roles of sporting giant, scientific man, and far-travelling explorer, promising plain names for plain things instead.

The book opens with a long voyage to the Cape, with porpoises, a shark, an albatross, Cape Town, Algoa Bay, and ox-wagon travel to the frontier. Hunting nearer home, where game had grown wild from disturbance, required patient search and long vigils, and Drayson recounts that slower sport in detail.
32909-zero-the-slaver-a-romance-of-equat:
Lawrence Fletcher's romance of equatorial Africa opens in Durban with a striking reward notice: one thousand pounds for news of Richard Grenville, a young Englishman last seen there in December 1877. In July 1880 a wiry, clean-shaved man in a rough grey suit stands before the notice with his back to the Standard Bank, while passersby pause, read, and move on. The missing man is the thread that pulls the reader inland.

From that street scene Fletcher builds a tale of slavers, pursuit, and African travel, in the adventurous manner of its period. The title figure, Zero the slaver, looms over a plot of capture, escape, and revenge. Modern readers will meet the prejudices of its age alongside its pace and color. The opening mystery still works: a fortune offered for one lost man, and a stranger who may know more than he says.
32912-into-the-unknown-a-romance-of-sout:
Lawrence Fletcher opens in a South African mountain pass, where two cousins rest with a Zulu chief. Alfred Leigh, second son of Lord Drelincourt, is a powerfully built young man of about twenty-five. His cousin Dick Grenville, aged thirty, has keen blue eyes and a resolute mouth. Their friend Myzukulwa stands six feet three inches, ringed and armed with club and spears.

The chapter is called The Ghosts' Pass, and danger arrives at once: Grenville spots a rifle barrel aimed at them from a fissure three hundred yards away. Later the party holds a rock against some three score attackers, who break and flee leaving upwards of a dozen men down. Myzukulwa's brother Amaxosa, left behind among witch-finders, fears for his father and sings a funereal wail. The romance follows loyalty tested in unknown country.
32914-tales-of-south-africa:
H. A. Bryden tells hunting and prospecting tales from the South African veldt, opening with the secret of Verloren Vlei. The narrator, Fairmount, first meets Koenraad du Plessis in the north of Waterberg. Du Plessis is a Transvaal Boer of Huguenot descent, shortish, dark, keen-eyed, and merry. The two men hunt together through a dry winter season in glorious game country.

At the end of July 1876 they meet again north-east of the Crocodile River, outspanned in a valley with a rare stream. Du Plessis recalls a kloof where he shot a white rhinoceros five years before, and natives who brought him a quill of gold. Later tales turn darker: a water-pit poisoned with euphorbia, six waterless days of travel, and a wagon left standing in the desert on the way to Tapinyani's kraal.
32923-my-kalulu-prince-king-and-slave-a-:
Henry M. Stanley's My Kalulu, Prince, King and Slave opens near Zanzibar. The household is that of Sheikh Amer bin Osman, a noble Arab of the Beni-Hassan tribe famed for charity and descent. The first chapter introduces his wife Amina, Arab councils, and the country of Rua. It also introduces a young consul's son, Selim, who argues with his mother before he is allowed to join an expedition sailing for Bagamoyo. Adventure, in Stanley's telling, begins at home.

Kalulu himself moves through the roles of the title, prince, king, and slave, as the story carries its characters into central Africa. Stanley draws on his own travels for color and detail, and the novel mixes exploration, captivity, and rescue in the manner of its age. Modern readers will note its colonial attitudes, but the tale's pace and its African settings still give it a strong pull.
33170-the-itching-palm-a-study-of-the-ha:
William R. Scott's Itching Palm, a study of the habit of tipping in America published in Philadelphia in 1916, takes a small custom and treats it as a social problem. Scott, author of The Americans in Panama, invites readers who approve or dispute his attitude toward tipping to write to him at Paducah, Kentucky. His chapters run from flunkyism in America and personal liberty, through Barbary pirates and personnel and distribution, to the economics, ethics, and psychology of tipping.

Later chapters cover the literature of tipping, tipping and the stage, employee and employer viewpoints, the sleeping-car phase, government and tipping, laws against tipping, Samuel Gompers on tipping, and the way out. Scott argues that tipping demeans both giver and receiver and distorts wages. The book remains a lively, opinionated study of an American habit that reformers of 1916 hoped to end, and it still speaks to debates about service pay.
33240-mammy-tittleback-and-her-family-a-:
Helen Jackson's cat stories, in a volume titled Cat Stories, include Mammy Tittleback and Her Family, a true story of seventeen cats, told with warmth and humor. Published in Boston in 1886, the book also holds Letters from a Cat and The Hunter Cats of Connorloa, all illustrated. Jackson, author of Ramona, writes of kittens who listen for hours as Johnny reads letters over to them.

The tales suit young readers and cat lovers alike, mixing feline antics with gentle lessons on care and kindness. Mammy Tittleback herself, a mother cat with a large family, anchors the book's charm. For those who enjoy animal stories from the Victorian age, this volume is a delightful, old-fashioned treat, full of purrs, pranks, and family feeling.
33508-a-new-subspecies-of-lizard-cnemido:
William E. Duellman describes a new subspecies of the lizard Cnemidophorus sacki from Michoacán, Mexico, in this 1960 paper from the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History. Earlier work had reviewed the western Mexican populations of the species but had not studied specimens from the Tepalcatepec Valley, the area between the ranges of two known subspecies.

Duellman examined large series of preserved specimens from that valley and found that its populations differ in scale pattern and coloration from other described forms. He therefore names and defines a distinct subspecies for the valley population, with two figures illustrating the account. The short paper is a precise example of mid-century reptile taxonomy built on field collecting and museum comparison.
33706-the-future-of-road-making-in-ameri:
Archer Butler Hulbert and others discuss the future of road-making in America in this 1905 symposium, volume fifteen of the Historic Highways of America series. The frontispiece honors General Roy Stone, father of the good-roads movement in the United States. Hulbert opens by observing that America has a future in road-building, and that its roads, covering perhaps a mile of travel for every citizen, are probably the poorest of any civilized nation.

Chapters treat government cooperation in object-lesson road work, good roads for farmers, the selection of materials for macadam roads, and stone roads in New Jersey. Illustrations show a good-roads train, a sample steel track, a typical macadam road near Bryn Mawr, grading, sand-clay roads in South Carolina, gravel near the Soldiers' Home, and an oyster-shell object-lesson road. The volume captures the progressive campaign for better rural roads.
33845-the-lightning-conductor-the-strang:
C. N. and A. M. Williamson edited this motor-car romance, published in New York in 1903 in a revised and enlarged edition. Molly Randolph writes letters home to her father from England, telling how she bought an automobile and set off with her aunt. A stay at Cobham, in Surrey, starts the tour.

The letters follow the car, its driver, and the people met on the road, with mishaps and flirtation along the way. The motor-car itself, nicknamed the Lightning Conductor, steals the show. The book captures the thrill of early motoring, when a road trip was still an adventure.
34028-races-and-immigrants-in-america:
John R. Commons, professor of political economy at the University of Wisconsin, wrote this study of race and immigration, published in New York in 1907. An Ellis Island picture fronts the book. Chapters move from race and democracy and colonial race elements through the Negro and nineteenth-century additions to industry, labor, and city life.

Later chapters treat crime and poverty, politics, and amalgamation and assimilation. Commons writes as a scholar of labor and public life, with maps and pictures of immigrant types. The book remains a key early study of how America absorbed new peoples.
34655-folk-stories-from-southern-nigeria:
Elphinstone Dayrell gathers tales in Folk Stories from Southern Nigeria, West Africa, printed in London and New York in 1910. Longmans Green made the book. Dayrell was district commissioner in Southern Nigeria. Andrew Lang writes an introduction. A Ju Ju mask from Ibo country, drawn in colour, fronts the volume.

The tortoise with a pretty daughter leads the tales. A hunter who obtained money from his friends the leopard, goat, bush cat, and cock, and got out of repaying them, follows. The woman with two skins and the king's magic drum stand in the run. Why the bat flies by night and why the fish lives in the water get their tales. The disobedient daughter who married a skull, and the elephant and the tortoise, fill out a thick set of beast tales and wonder tales.
34667-the-vee-boers-a-tale-of-adventure-:
The Vee Boers is a tale of adventure in southern Africa by Captain Mayne Reid, in an edition dated 1907 from Routledge of London. Vee Boers were cattle farmers of Dutch stock who roved the plains. Reid opens on the Karoo, a vast dry plain.

The plain runs flat to the sky line, bare of trees save a lone camel thorn or a clump of aloes. Tufts of white, withered grass show how sterile the land is. Three huge wagons roll over it, each with eight pairs of long horned oxen. A driver cracks a whip like a fishing rod, a man on foot bears the jambok, and a foreloper leads the team. The owners ride ahead, Jan Van Dorn, Hans Blom, and Klaas Rynwald. Boys got wild land, beasts, and peril in Reid bold style.
348-hesiod-the-homeric-hymns-and-homeric:
This volume gathers Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and the lesser Homerica in English translation. Contents run from Works and Days and the Theogony through the Shield of Heracles and the Catalogues of Women. Hymns to Dionysus, Demeter, Apollo, Hermes, and Aphrodite follow.

An introduction covers the Boeotian and Ionic schools, the Trojan cycle, and the contest of Homer and Hesiod. Fragments, epigrams, and burlesque poems close the set, with a bibliography. The book gives readers the full archaic Greek shelf beyond Homer. It serves students and lovers of myth. Hesiod's farmer calendar still speaks to readers of work and seasons.
34893-beautiful-gardens-in-america:
Louise Shelton wrote Beautiful Gardens in America, for Scribner. A second edition came out at New York in 1916. The book is a large illustrated volume, priced at five dollars. The Garden and its Meaning opens its contents list. Climate in America takes the second chapter of the book.

New England follows, state by state, in the contents after that. Maine, New Hampshire with Vermont, and Massachusetts stand there. Rhode Island takes its own pages in the same survey. A Newport garden fronts the book as its first plate. That place is photographed in colour for the frontispiece. In green old gardens hidden away, its dedication verse runs. Married to pleasure and buried to pain, the verses dream. Continuous Bloom in America stands as her companion volume. Shelton gives the republic's great gardens their portrait album.
34974-the-simple-cobler-of-aggawam-in-am:
The Simple Cobler of Aggawam in America is a sharp tract of sixteen forty seven. Its shown name is Theodore de la Guard, a mask for the church man Nathaniel Ward. Ward was born at Haverhill in England in fifteen seventy and trained at Cambridge. He read law, roamed the main land, then turned to church work. The tract prints a shoe mend trade as its key sign for state craft.

The cobler begs to patch his torn home land with all the stitch skill he has. He asks no pay for the work by old English wont, the page jokes. Latin tags from Cicero line the front leaf with jest verse. A life note in the text names Ward as friend of the first New England folk. The tract speaks from London in a year of civil war strain.
35234-the-progress-of-ethnology-an-accou:
The Progress of Ethnology is an account of fresh research in many parts of the globe, by John Russell Bartlett. Its full title ties the work to the physical history of man. Bartlett was secretary of the American Ethnological Society and of the New York Historical Society. This second edition came out in New York in 1847 from Bartlett and Welford.

The contents open with North America. Fresh digs and finds in the mounds and other earthworks of Ohio stand first in the list. Kindred research and its results in Mississippi and Louisiana stand next. The work gathers reports of digging, of tongues, and of travel that bear on the races of man and their past. It is a survey of the young science of its day, drawn from the labors of men in the field.
35245-the-world-and-its-people-book-vii-:
Views in Africa is book seven of The World and Its People, a school reading series edited by Larkin Dunton, head master of the Boston Normal School. The series was made to add to the common school readers, its front pages say. It gives practice in reading while backing up school study with sound facts and choice pieces from the best writing.

The set runs from stories of child life at home, at play, in the country, and at school, to books on the world at large. Our own country, our American neighbours, modern Europe, and life in Asia precede this volume. Book seven turns to Africa, in more than one part. Pupils of its day thus read their way outward from the home to the far continents, one shelf of small volumes at a time.
35473-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Ethiopia to Evangelical Associations is one alphabetic stretch of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, the famous edition of 1910 and 1911. A transcriber's notes at the front explain the plain text dress: small numbers set low in the print become marked figures, accents are dropped, and side notes now serve as paragraph titles. Three corrected misprints are listed by article.

Within this stretch fall such articles as Euboea, on the long Greek island, and Eucharist, on the sacrament of the altar. The note on Eucharist quotes the words of the covenant from Matthew's gospel. An article on Eudaemonism, the doctrine that happiness is the chief good, follows in the same pages. The eleventh edition is still prized for the depth and style of its longer articles.
35658-voyages-from-montreal-through-the-:
Alexander Mackenzie tells of his voyages from Montreal through North America to the Frozen and Pacific Oceans in 1789 and 1793. An account of the rise and state of the fur trade stands with the tale. This first volume comes from a New York edition of 1903, with a map. An introduction gives the life of the explorer.

Mackenzie was born at Inverness in Scotland about 1755 and came to North America while young. He learned the fur trade in the counting-house of Gregory and Company, tied to the North-West Company. A small venture to Detroit sent him into the back country to open trade. Later years took him over plains, down rapids of unknown rivers, and across hard mountain ranges.
35659-voyages-from-montreal-through-the-:
Alexander Mackenzie tells his voyages from Montreal across North America here. Barnes printed volume two in New York in 1903 with a map. The voyages reached the Frozen and Pacific Oceans in 1789 and 1793. An account of the fur trade rise and state joins them.

Chapter one moves the party from tent to house for winter. Hardships, a violent hurricane, and a cured Indian wound follow there. Customs on a death, a gaming quarrel, and murder fill the chapter. Rocky Mountain Indians and spring signs close its long summary. Alexander Mackenzie made the two great journeys himself.
35791-babylonian-assyrian-birth-omens-an:
Babylonian-Assyrian Birth-Omens and Their Cultural Significance is a study by Morris Jastrow Jr. Jastrow taught Semitic languages at the University of Pennsylvania. The book came out at Giessen in 1914. It asks how the peoples of Babylonia and Assyria read the future in strange births. Jastrow sets birth-omens beside two other great methods, hepatoscopy and astrology.

The study works through the omen collections kept in Ashurbanapal's library. Animal omens cover twins, double foetuses, and malformed ears. Human omens cover multiple births, misshapen limbs, and infants with animal features. Jastrow then traces the ideas into Greek and Roman writers. He closes with physiognomy, fabulous beasts, and the sphinx. The volume is dedicated to Sir William Osler of Oxford.
35941-the-life-of-saint-monica:
Frances Alice Forbes wrote The Life of Saint Monica, issued in a third edition by Burns, Oates and Washbourne in London in 1928. The book belongs to Standard-bearers of the Faith, a series of saints' lives for young and old. Church approval pages date from 1915. Forbes calls the book above all the story of a mother.

Monica was raised by Christian parents at Tagaste in North Africa and married into the pagan household of Patricius. By gentleness and charity she won her husband and his mother to Christ. The greater trial was her son Augustine, who left the faith and slipped away to Rome. The life follows her prayers to Milan, his baptism, and her death at Ostia on the way home.
36024-north-america:
Israel Russell, professor of geology at the University of Michigan, wrote North America as one volume of Appletons' World Series, The Regions of the World. H J Mackinder of Oxford shaped the series, whose other volumes treat Britain, Africa, India, and Russia. Appleton issued Russell's book at New York in 1904, with maps and diagrams. A relief map of the continent, from a photograph, stands at the front.

The early chapters treat the margin of the continent: the shelf under the sea, the coasts, the islands, and the harbors. Later parts take up the lay of the land, from coastal plains and the Atlantic ranges to the great basin and the Pacific ranges, and then the climate in its zones. Russell writes as a working geologist for the general reader, in clear, ordered prose.
36198-the-mystery-of-the-barranca:
The Mystery of the Barranca is a novel by Herman Whitaker. Harper and Brothers held the rights and printed it in February 1913. Whitaker had written The Planter and The Settler before this tale. He gives the book to Vera, his daughter and gentle collaborator. A front picture shows Seyd lifting Francesca in a daring leap.

The tale opens at a small station deep in the interior of Mexico. Billy Thornton laughs at two stout men embracing in fond greeting. Two years in Mexico had used his friend Robert Seyd to the sight. Peons in white blankets and rancheros in leather crowd the platform scene. Hacendados, the estate owners, stand out in that bright mixed throng. Mines and mining tools ride with the two young Americans there. Francesca and her great wolf hound step into the tale early.
3620-geological-observations-on-south-am:
Charles Darwin writes a scientific volume from his voyage on the Beagle, covering the geology of South America. Chapters treat the elevation of the eastern and western coasts and the plains and valleys of Chile. They also cover salty surface deposits, the formations of the Pampas, and the older tertiary rocks of Patagonia and Chile. Darwin begins with upraised shells at La Plata and Bahia Blanca, and with the step formed plains of Patagonia.

The book argues that whole coasts have risen slowly from the sea, leaving shells far inland and terraces along the shore. Darwin writes with close observation of rocks, fossils, and landforms. It suits readers interested in geology, in the Beagle voyage, and in the fieldwork that shaped Darwin's view of a changing earth.
36578-the-warden-of-the-plains-and-other:
The Warden of the Plains gathers stories of life in the Canadian North-West by John Maclean, printed at Toronto in 1896. Maclean also wrote Canadian Savage Folk. Laughlin drew the pictures. Twelve tales fill the contents, from the title story to The Coming of Apauakas.

The first tale opens at a roundup camp at the base of the Rocky Mountains. Where buffalo once fed in countless herds, the white man's cattle roam in tens of thousands. Cowboy Bill greets a rider who seems to spring from the prairie itself. Jake, the only preacher the fellows have, is welcome in camp. Maclean mixes missionary work with plains life.
36831-a-tree-with-a-bird-in-it-a-symposi:
Margaret Widdemer, who wrote Factories and The Old Road to Paradise, made this odd book of poems. Harcourt, Brace printed it at New York in 1922, with drawings by William Saphier. Its full title calls it a gathering of present-day American poets.

The seed of the book is one sight: a pear tree with a grackle on it. Poet after poet was shown that tree and bird, and each wrote what the sight stirred. Their verse, set side by side, shows how wide one small scene can spread in many minds. Widdemer's own frame holds the set. The book is at once a game, a test, and a portrait of a young school of American song.
3699-miss-sarah-jack-of-spanish-town-jam:
Anthony Trollope sets this tale in Jamaica at a time when the island's sugar wealth was fading and its great houses felt the pinch. Miss Sarah Jack, a strong willed spinster of Spanish Town, makes an annual round of the estates, and on one visit she brings a suitor in tow for young Marian's sake. Her host Maurice, busy turning cane into sugar and rum, resents the meddling even as he blushes at her plain talk.

The story pairs a fading colony with a sharp domestic comedy, as green valleys and fine old houses frame plain questions about money, marriage, and who may speak for a young woman. Miss Jack means well and oversteps at every turn. Readers get both a portrait of a colony in decline and a brisk contest of wills between a matchmaker and a proud young planter.
37116-history-of-the-buccaneers-of-ameri:
History of the Buccaneers of America, by James Burney, captain in the Royal Navy, was printed in London for Payne and Foss in 1816. The opening chapters lay the ground in Spanish America before the buccaneers themselves appear.

Chapter one considers the rights gained by discovering unknown lands, and the claims the Spaniards built on them. Chapter two reviews Spanish dominion in Hayti, or Hispaniola, where Columbus first governed. Dogs used against the Indians, massacres, and heavy tribute are recorded. The repartimientos, the mines, and the first Africans carried to the West Indies follow. Las Casas and Cardinal Ximenes tried to serve the Indians. Later chapters turn to the cattle hunters of Hispaniola. The Brethren of the Coast, the seizing of Tortuga, and the origin of the name buccaneer follow from them.
37260-the-outspan-tales-of-south-africa:
Percy Fitzpatrick told these outspan tales of South Africa from the fields. Heinemann printed the edition dated 1897 in London for readers. Chapter one opens in a prospector hut on a yarn swapping night. Snakes, hunting, lucky strikes, and escapes had run dry by then.

A man told of meeting a stranger he felt he had seen before. They compared dates and places ten years back, still puzzled both. The other had once stood in a devil of a fright somewhere. A ticket taken at the wrong bridge end held the key.
37265-an-i-d-b-in-south-africa:
An I D B in South Africa is a novel by Louise Vescelius-Sheldon. The John W Lovell Company published this edition in New York in 1888. G E Graves and Al Hencke illustrated it. The title's initials stand for illicit diamond buying, a crime of the Kimberley fields. The first chapter is named The Marked Diamond. It opens at the theatre.

Major Kildare and Herr Schwatka watch the boxes at the Theatre Royal, Kimberley. Schwatka identifies the beautiful Mrs Laure and her husband Donald. Miss Kate Darcy, an American visitor, sits with them. Count Telfus, a large dealer in diamonds, completes the party. The marked diamond of the title waits behind the theatricals. Diamonds, beauty, and secret parentage set the Kimberley plot in motion.
37472-zanzibar-tales-told-by-natives-of-:
Zanzibar Tales is a set of folk tales told by the folk of the east coast of Africa, turned from the tongue of that coast by Bateman. Pictures by a named hand fill its form. It came out at Chicago in the first year of the last age.

His word at the front sets the scene. Thirty years past, he says, the heart of Africa was a land no map knew. Now its main marks are well known. Then as now, the wee isle of Zanzibar, just south of the line, was the start place of all trips to the inlands. Its big town was where the gear for the plunge in was made ready. The tales keep the voice of the men who told them.
37544-cupid-in-africa:
Cupid in Africa, by Wren, first published in 1920, is a comic war novel by the author of Beau Geste. It follows Bertram Greene, the soft son of the stiff and unlucky Major Hugh Walsingham Greene. Three parts trace the making of Bertram, his baking by war, and his baking by love.

Sent to East Africa in the Great War, Bertram endures Mombasa, convoys, hunger, and a trial, then faces love in the shape of his father's runaway second wife. Wren mixes barracks humor with real campaign detail. The book shows the lighter side of the colonial war story he later made famous.
37823-neotropical-hylid-frogs-genus-smil:
Neotropical Hylid Frogs, Genus Smilisca, by William Duellman and Linda Trueb, is a scientific monograph from the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History, published July 14, 1966. It runs nearly a hundred pages with twelve plates and seventeen figures. The authors examined 4,151 preserved frogs, plus skeletons, tadpoles, and eggs.

Six species get full accounts, among them one new to science, and keys sort both adults and tadpoles. Later parts weigh bones, muscles, skin, breeding calls, and family ties. Field work in Mexico and Central America across a decade stands behind the tables. It is taxonomy done the slow, thorough way.
38131-on-secret-service-detective-myster:
William Nelson Taft wrote On Secret Service, published in nineteen twenty-one, a set of detective tales with a twist. Each tale rests on a real case solved by agents of the United States government. Harper and Brothers issued the book at New York and London.

Cases range from a mint mystery and a smuggler to a secret still and a poison-pen puzzle. One tale turns on thirty thousand yards of silk, and another on a clue in a small ad column. A girl at a switchboard, a man with three wives, and a lost sum of money all feature. Short frames set up each case.
38165-the-cabin-la-barraca:
The Cabin is the English translation of La Barraca, a novel by Vicente Blasco Ibanez. Alfred Knopf of New York published it in 1919, in his Borzoi Spanish translations series. Francis Haffkine Snow and Beatrice Mekota translated the book, and John Garrett Underhill wrote the introduction.

Five printings appeared within the first year, a sign of the Spanish author's American vogue. The story opens on the Valencian plain at dawn. Nightingales finish their songs as light breaks toward the sea, and flocks of sparrows rise like pursued urchins. The barraca of the title is the farm cabin at the tale's heart. Blasco Ibanez built his fame on novels of his native region's soil and strife. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
39893-defenseless-america:
Hudson Maxim sounds the alarm in Defenseless America, from Hearst's International Library Company of New York, copyrighted in 1915. A motto fronts the book: the quick-firing gun is the greatest life-saving instrument ever invented. Maxim presented copies with his compliments to a few selected leaders of American thought and shapers of public opinion.

His letter to the reader asks to be convinced of the defenseless state of the country, and convinced that the danger is as great as the weakness. He urges preparation against war to safeguard property, honor, lives, and the sanctity of the American home. A fifty-cent edition spreads the call.
39984-lord-loveland-discovers-america:
Williamson and his wife wrote this novel, copyrighted by Doubleday in New York in 1910. Four illustrations in color by Brehm brighten the tale of an English lord abroad. A plate shows Loveland tucking a wind-blown rug round the feet of his namesake's niece, by its caption.

The discovery of America by Lord Loveland opens the contents at page three. Between Betty and Jim and the inestimable Foxham follow in the chapter list.
