The Williamsons filled shelves with motor-car romances of Europe, and here they turn the joke around, bringing a lord to discover America and an American girl.
41217-english-french-and-french-english-:
English French and French English Dictionary of the Motor Car, Cycle and Boat is a technical word book by Frederick Lucas. Spon published the new impression at London and New York in 1915. The English French part runs to page ninety five, where the French English part begins. Entries march in strict order from the accelerator onward.

Accelerator is rendered as its French twin, with its control gear, pedal, rod, spring, washer, sector, and shaft each given in turn. Accessories, accident, and accumulator follow, with the cap of the accumulator after them. Air chamber, air inlet pipe, and air lever show the engine age arriving. Such dictionaries served the cross channel motor trade, when British and French makers led the new industry. A motorist in France, or a mechanic with a French car, could name every part. The book preserves the young motor age's vocabulary in two tongues.
41697-merck-s-1899-manual-of-the-materia:
Merck and Company issued Merck's 1899 Manual of the Materia Medica at New York, with a calendar for 1899 at its head. A motto says each gain in true knowledge is a gain in human power. Front pages advertise the firm's analytic laboratories in New York. Tests of water, milk, blood, urine, and food are offered to doctors.

Prices are listed for common tests in plain figures. A sputum test for tuberculosis bacilli costs three dollars. A urine test for one constituent costs one dollar fifty. Water fitness tests cost ten dollars and a typhoid germ search costs twenty five. The manual proper then lists drugs and their uses for doctors and druggists. Dose, form, and action are given in brief entries in letter order. The book is a working desk guide of its year.
41806-impressions-of-america:
Impressions of America, by Oscar Wilde, was shaped by Stuart Mason and printed by the Keystone Press at Sunderland in 1906. The edition ran to five hundred copies, fifty of them on hand made paper. Wilde gives the book to Walter Ledger as a pledge of friendship.

Two poems, Le Jardin and La Mer, stand at the front of the head. The first tells of the lily withered chalice and the last wood pigeon calling from the beech trees. The second shows a white mist across the shrouds and a wild moon like an angry lion eye. The preface then tells that Oscar Wilde visited America in the year 1882. Interest in the aesthetic school, of which he was already a leader, drew crowds. On landing in New York he was bombarded by journalists eager to interview the distinguished stranger.
42032-the-trail-of-the-seneca:
The Trail of the Seneca, by James Braden, was published in 1907. Vosburgh drew the pictures. Braden had written Connecticut Boys in the Western Reserve and other frontier tales. A stone hatchet on the narrator's table opens the tale. It recalls Captain Pipe, Fishing Bird, and Big Buffalo. The true center here is Lone-Elk, a Seneca cast out from his people's villages. Bold, crafty, and vain, he drives the plot.

Chapter heads promise a witchcraft death sentence and a hidden lead mine. Salt springs, a hidden tomahawk, and an explosion follow. A meeting with Mad Anthony and a cabin burning raise the stakes. The last heads ask who killed Big Buffalo. Boys of the day got a fast tale of Delaware and Seneca lands.
43429-cats-their-points-and-characterist:
Cats, their points and characteristics, with curiosities of cat life and a chapter on cat ailments, is a cat book by Gordon Stables, a naval doctor. Stables had written of medical life in the navy and of wild adventures in the far north. A picture called Shipmates fronts the volume. The contents open with an apology, then pussy on her native hearth.

Pussy's love of children, a cat called Poll, and the wisdom of cats fill the early chapters. A cat that keeps the sabbath, honest cats, and a ploughman's cat called Mysie follow. Tenacity of life in cats, wandering in cats, and whether cats can be trusted come in turn. Pussy as a mother, home ties, and fishing exploits close the visible list. Stables writes as a lover and doctor of animals both.
43935-william-e-burton-actor-author-and-:
William E. Burton: Actor, Author, and Manager is a sketch of a stage life by William L. Keese. It came out in New York and London in 1885 from G. P. Putnam's Sons, with pictures. The book is inscribed to the daughters of Burton, friends of the author for many years. Its preface states the gap the book aims to fill.

No fit account of the late William E. Burton had been given to the public, Keese holds. In his life no man was better known, he says. His death drew out a broad show of praise for his gifts and of grief at his loss. The press notices of his death gave some short detail, and the book builds a full record from the memory of his work on the stage.
44075-embassy-to-the-eastern-courts-of-c:
Embassy to the Eastern Courts of Cochin-China, Siam, and Muscat, by Edmund Roberts, was published at New York in 1837 by Harper and Brothers. Roberts sailed in the United States sloop-of-war Peacock, under Commander David Geisinger, during the years 1832 to 1834, to make treaties with eastern powers. He inscribes the volume to Levi Woodbury.

The introduction tells how the mission began. Roberts, acquainted with the commerce of Asia, wrote to Woodbury, then a senator. His letter told of the neglected state of American trade, and of the heavier duties laid on it beside English commerce. Woodbury became secretary of the navy. News then came that the ship Friendship of Salem had been plundered, and much of her crew murdered, by the natives of Qualah Battu. The pepper trade of Sumatra stood endangered.
44919-discourses-in-america:
Matthew Arnold prints three discourses given in America in a volume issued in London in 1885. The first, on Numbers, was first given in New York and then printed in the Nineteenth Century. The second began as the Rede Lecture at Cambridge and was recast for American hearers.

The third treats Emerson and was given at Boston, in what Arnold calls Emerson's own delightful town. In his preface Arnold thanks his American audiences for hearing a speaker who did not flatter them. He stands by his praise of American institutions while keeping his caution, drawn from the rule that moral causes govern the rise and fall of states. Readers get Arnold's famed terms, Barbarians and Philistines, applied to England and America alike.
46692-caudebec-in-america:
William Louis Cuddeback, a physician, compiled this genealogy, printed at New York in 1919: a record of the descendants of Jacques Caudebec from 1700 to 1920. The frontispiece explains the family coat-of-arms in full heraldic detail.

The shield is azure with three silver smelts, a daisy near the point, and a wreath of laurel and olive for peace and victory. Cuddeback dedicates the book to his wife of more than thirty-five years. His motto for the chase is frankly stated: man is a hunting animal, and he is fond of hunting out a pedigree. The contents promise a family chart, deeds, and the home of the first settler at Pioneer Knoll. Descendants get their Huguenot line documented.
47457-jaros-hygienic-wear-the-therapeuti:
Jaros Hygienic Wear sets out how health underwear can treat illness and keep it away, in a fourth edition that came out in New York in 1890. The Jaros company wrote the book for doctors. A portrait of Professor Pettenkofer, head of the Hygienic Institute at Munich, lends the science weight.

Sections treat health clothing, the ideas behind clothing, and the underwear itself, with letters of praise at the end. The text leans on Pettenkofer, Parkes, and Buck, whose ideas linked cloth types to health. Wool comes first among fibres. A close view shows wool fibre as a tube of cells with scales that lie over each other. The pamphlet is part health case, part trade writing for a health garment.
48182-the-sabbath-a-paper-read-at-the-co:
The Sabbath is a paper by Andrew Thomson of Edinburgh, read at Geneva on the second of September 1861. Thomson spoke at the conference of the Evangelical Alliance held in that city. The paper was printed at London in 1863 and reached a huge sale. The title page marks this copy as the 430th thousand.

A preface by Ryle, an English clergyman, commends the paper to readers. Ryle was asked to back the Scottish case on the Sabbath with a few words. The paper defends the strict keeping of the Lord’s day, in the Scottish manner. Thomson spoke for a church that held Sunday rest as a divine law. The vast printing shows how live the question was in Victorian Britain. Railway travel and Sunday work pressed on the old rest, and this paper pushed back.
48409-myths-and-legends-of-british-north:
Myths and Legends of British North America was selected and edited by Katharine Berry Judson. McClurg printed it at Chicago in 1917, and it came out that April. A frontispiece shows Haida totem poles, the genealogical trees of the Haida.

The tales are sorted by tellers, tribe by tribe. Haida, Eastern Eskimo, and Bella Coola beliefs open the book. Creation tales follow from the Wyandot, the Cree, and the Thompson River people. Raven works through the Haida set, making the world and winning light. Origins of light and fire recur in Carrier, Lillooet, and Shuswap tellings. Grizzly Bear and Coyote make the light and the seasons. Sun and moon tales run from the Ojibwa to the Central Eskimo. Sisters escape Skyland, the Pleiades rise, and the summer comes, before the close.
48856-the-emancipation-of-south-america:
William Pilling cut down and turned into English the great history of San Martin written by Bartolomé Mitre, first president of the Argentine Republic. Chapman and Hall of London published the shorter book in 1893, with maps. Pilling says in his preface that he has trimmed the parts that touch San Martin alone. He gives the weight to the events of the age.

So read, the book is a history of how South America threw off Spain. Two lives run through it, those of San Martin and of Bolívar. The first chapter sweeps from the settling of Spanish America to the first throes of revolt. Pilling aimed at the general reader, not the student. He left the full store of notes and proof to the Spanish original, and kept the stir and sweep of the tale.
49410-the-works-of-garcilasso-de-la-vega:
The Works of Garcilasso de la Vega is an English verse translation of the Spanish poet surnamed the Prince of Castilian Poets. Wiffen translated the poems and wrote the life and a critical essay on Spanish poetry. Hurst and Robinson published the book in London in 1823. A portrait shows Garcilasso, born in 1503 and dead in 1536.

The title page quotes Byron turning the pages of Boscán or Garcilasso. Wiffen dedicates the translation to the duke of Bedford. Garcilasso brought the Italian sonnet and the new measures into Spanish verse before his early death in war. His eclogues and sonnets shaped all later Spanish poetry. This volume made him known to English readers.
49491-the-sunny-south-an-autumn-in-spain:
The Sunny South is a travel book by Captain J W Clayton, late of the Thirteenth Hussars. Hurst and Blackett published it in London in 1869. The subtitle calls it an autumn in Spain and Majorca.

The route runs through Rouen, Tours, Bordeaux, and Biarritz into Spain. Chapters cover Burgos, Valladolid, Madrid, and the Balearic island. Clayton notes cathedrals, inns, customs officers, and street scenes. He drew the views himself, including one of Barcelona. British officers often published such tour accounts. This one records Spain just before rail travel changed the journey for good.
49637-account-of-the-russian-discoveries:
An Account of the Russian Discoveries between Asia and America was written by William Coxe and printed in London in 1780. Coxe was a fellow of King's College, Cambridge. To the voyage accounts the title page adds the conquest of Siberia and a history of the transactions and commerce between Russia and China.

The preface explains the research. The late Russian discoveries had engaged the curiosity of the public, and during a stay at Petersburg Coxe directed his inquiries to learning what new light had been thrown on them. He sought the journals of the several voyages made after the expedition of Beering and Tschirikoff in 1741, where Muller had closed his account of the first Russian navigations. A German treatise printed at Hamburg and Leipsic in 1776, compiled from the original journals, gave the voyages from 1745 to 1770, and Muller himself vouched for its exactness.
50045-the-art-of-kissing-curiously-histo:
The Art of Kissing, Curiously, Historically, Humorously, Poetically Considered, was held in 1902 by Will Rossiter and issued at New York by J S Ogilvie. The book is given to all who love. Pictures show a sly kiss at seven, a nicer kiss at seventeen, and the same game at seventy. Three verses on those ages head the work.

Part One treats the origin of kissing and a Scandinavian tradition. Kissing in ancient Rome and among the Jews and early Christians follows. Biblical kissing and its religious sense get space. Early England customs as told by Erasmus and the views of John Bunyan sit side by side. How Adam kissed Eve is weighed with jest. Definitions from the dictionary, Shakespeare, Herrick, Sidney, and Coleridge close the survey. A grammar of kissing and a science of why kisses please end the part.
50828-the-bark-canoes-and-skin-boats-of-:
Bark Canoes and Skin Boats of North America is a museum study by Edwin Tappan Adney and Howard Chapelle. The Smithsonian Institution issued it at Washington in 1964 as Bulletin 230 of the National Museum. Chapelle was curator of transportation at the museum, as the title page states. More than two hundred illustrations accompany the text of the study.

The book treats the bark canoes of the woodland peoples and the skin boats of the northern coasts. Adney, who had built and studied canoes since his youth in New Brunswick, supplied the field knowledge. Together they fixed the forms, materials, and building ways of craft that were vanishing from the water. Boat builders still loft canoes and kayaks from these pages. The bulletin is a salvage record, made by two men who knew that a boat is a document that sinks if no one draws it in time.
50954-the-complete-poetic-and-dramatic-w:
The Complete Poetic and Dramatic Works of Robert Browning holds his verse in one book. Horace Scudder shaped this Cambridge set of the poets for home shelves. A front print shows Asolo, the town in Italy the poet called home. Rights date the work to the year eighteen ninety five.

The note says a full set in six parts had first come out in eighteen eighty seven. A fresh English set then set the text right by the poets last hand. Aids to study the hard verse were drawn up for this new print. Long verse tales and stage plays fill the fat one book set. Browning ranks as a chief voice of his age in dense, bold verse.
5123-the-contest-in-america:
John Stuart Mill's essay, reprinted from Fraser's Magazine, addresses Britain during the American Civil War. Mill warns that the real contest is not only between North and South but between free government and slavery. He argues that British sympathy for the Confederacy would betray the cause of liberty itself.

Written while war still raged and Anglo-American tension ran high, the essay presses readers to judge the conflict by its moral stakes rather than by trade or pride. It stands as a clear example of Mill's political writing: reasoned, urgent, and willing to tell his own countrymen an unwelcome truth.
51746-my-reminiscences-of-east-africa:
My Reminiscences of East Africa is the war memoir of General von Lettow-Vorbeck, printed at London by Hurst and Blackett. The book carries a portrait of the general, twenty-two maps and sketch-maps, and thirteen drawings by his adjutant. Lettow-Vorbeck commanded the German protective force in East Africa through the First World War. His reminiscences give the German side of that campaign.

The war opens with mobilization, English consul activity, and defence of the coastal towns. First actions follow: the bombardment of the wireless tower at Dar-es-Salaam, the cruiser Königsberg, and the capture of Taveta. Attacks on the British Uganda Railway and the November actions at Tanga come next. At Tanga the landing corps fights at Ras-Kasone, then meets a counter-attack and flees. Lettow-Vorbeck was the only German commander unbeaten at the armistice.
51932-journal-of-a-residence-in-america:
Frances Anne Butler, in the theatre Fanny Kemble, keeps a diary in Journal of a Residence in America, printed at Paris in 1835. Galignani made the book, in one volume. She writes as an English stage player touring the young republic.

Her preface lowers expectations with care. Curiosity in England about America runs high, she grants: its political existence is a momentous experiment, watched by many anxious eyes. Other travellers have told of customs, manners, and scenery, she notes. She has neither the intention nor the capability of adding detail of interest to theirs. The book is what it professes to be, she insists: her personal journal, and not a history or a description of men and manners in the United States.
52812-the-story-of-majorca-and-minorca:
The Story of Majorca and Minorca is a history of the Balearic Islands by Sir Clements Markham, geographer and historian, published in London by Smith, Elder in 1908, with two maps. Markham had written lives of Richard the Third, Lord Fairfax, and Edward the Sixth.

The first part treats Majorca. It opens with King Jayme the First of Aragon, and how he resolved to conquer Majorca and drive out the Moors. His victory over the Moors and his siege of the capital follow. He conquered the whole island and became its first Christian king. His last visits, the settlement of the island, and his death close his story. Then the kings of Aragon take up the tale: a glove taken up for Conradin, the Pope's curses coming home to roost, and Pedro keeping his tryst. Markham tells island history as a chain of kings and fleets.
5327-pinocchio-in-africa:
Pinocchio in Africa, translated from the Italian of Cherubini by Angelo Patri, sends Collodi's wooden boy on a new adventure. Chapters explain why Pinocchio did not go to school, follow him welcoming a circus, among wild animals. He makes friends with them, and then the chapters carry him, determined, to Africa, bidding goodbye to the animals.

Patri, a New York school principal, translated the book for American children, with drawings by Charles Copeland. Readers get a sequel of sorts to Pinocchio, in which the puppet's mischief and curiosity carry him from schoolroom truancy to an African journey.
53276-the-every-day-book-and-table-book-:
The Every Day Book and Table Book, volume two of three, is a calendar work by William Hone. Its long title calls it an everlasting calendar of popular amusements and customs. It covers sports, pastimes, ceremonies, manners, and events for each day of the year. The set aims to form a full history of the year, months, and seasons.

Weather notes, rules for health and conduct, and tales fill its pages in turn. Facts and notices range across chronology, old customs, place lore, and lives of note. Natural history, art, science, and general letters all find a place here. Verse pieces are mixed in for daily use and pastime reading. The volume holds hundreds of engravings and opens with the clog almanack. Hone dedicates this volume to the earl of Darlington for his love of old sports.
53430-principia-ethica:
George Moore, the Cambridge philosopher, wrote this founding book on ethics in English. Cambridge University Press issued Principia Ethica, with Macmillan selling it in New York. Moore was a fellow of the British Academy and a lecturer at Cambridge, the title page records in his honors.

Moore asks what good means and argues that it cannot be defined by anything else. Calling good the same as pleasure, or as what is desired, commits what he names the naturalistic fallacy, in his famous claim. Generations of philosophers argued inside the frame this quiet, rigorous book built for the study of right and good.
53574-life-in-south-africa:
Life in South Africa is Lady Barker’s account of her years at the Cape, told in dated pieces. James B Lippincott and Company issued the book in Philadelphia in eighteen hundred seventy seven. Barker had written Station Life in New Zealand. Part one opens aboard the Edinburgh Castle in October eighteen hundred seventy five.

Twenty four days of sea and sky end at Cape Town. Heat at the line drove the crew near despair at first. Then cold winds struck, and the line was crossed in great coats. Table Mountain hid in fog till the ship lay in its lee. Robben Island showed as a dun hill in the dusk. Heat, glare, and gray fog mark her first keen notes. The Cape years then unfold in fresh dated entries.
53755-the-taleef-shereef-or-indian-mater:
Taleef Shereef, or Indian Materia Medica, is a medical work translated by George Playfair. The Medical and Physical Society of Calcutta published the book in that city. It was printed at the Baptist Mission Press on Circular Road for the society. Playfair was superintending surgeon in the Bengal service of the East India Company.

A transcriber notice warns that the medical knowledge in the book is several centuries old in its matter. The publication is for historical interest only, and is not medical advice, the notice states. The work is a translation of a Persian treatise on the drugs of India in its origin. It sets out the plants, minerals, and preparations of the bazaars with their uses in native practice. The book is a meeting of two medicines on paper, Persian learning in English dress for the Bengal surgeon.
54266-history-of-the-indians-of-north-an:
Goodrich, known as the author of Peter Parley's Tales, wrote this history, published at Boston in 1844. Goodrich entered the book for copyright in Massachusetts that year in his own name. An introduction opens the work, and the origin of the aborigines follows as the first main topic.

Classification of the Indians, the peoples of the West Indies and the Caribs come next in the contents. Early Mexican history and Mexico after the conquest fill later chapters in the list. Goodrich writes for young readers in the Parley manner, though his terms and judgments reflect the views of his age and nation.
54400-alone-in-west-africa:
A travel memoir by Mary Gaunt, published in 1911. Scribner's issued it in New York, and T Werner Laurie in London. Gaunt travelled alone through West Africa as a widow. Her dedication thanks a long chain of helpers. Colonial Office letters opened the way for her. Elder Dempster gave her a free passage. Captains, officials, and traders of several nations smoothed the road.

Her first chapter traces a hereditary taste for wandering. An ancestor served the East India Company and colonised Van Diemen's Land. Ballarat and Warrnambool shaped her Australian years. Marriage, widowhood, and thin literary earnings in London follow. At last she boards the Gando for the Gambia. The book records a lone woman's journey up the Volta.
54635-my-life-in-china-and-america:
My Life in China and America, published in 1909, is Yung Wing's memoir of a life split between two worlds. Yung Wing was born on November 17, 1828, at Nam Ping, a village near Macao. He was the third of four children and the only one still living when he wrote. A missionary's wife opened a school at Macao, and her manager, a friend of his father, got the boy in.

The chapters follow him to America, to Monson Academy and through college. Back in China he hunted a post, traded, and visited the Taipings. His great work was the Chinese Educational Mission, which sent Chinese boys to study in America. He also investigated the coolie traffic in Peru. The recall to China and the coup of 1898 close the story.
54663-catalogue-of-rudimentary-scientifi:
James S Virtue issued this catalogue from City Road and Ivy Lane after buying all of the books of Mr Weale. It lists cheap works on science, school subjects, and the classics, made for colleges and for high and ordinary schools. The same books were meant for mechanics' institutions and free libraries, and for readers who taught themselves at home.

The Rudimentary Series dominates the list, and its numbered volumes sold for a shilling or two each. Charles Tomlinson wrote on natural philosophy, mechanics, and pneumatics, while Portlock wrote on geology. George Field gave a grammar of colouring, and other books took up book-keeping, arithmetic, astronomy, and glass work. Taken as a whole, the catalogue is a clear record of cheap self-education in full working order.
54746-quaint-and-historic-forts-of-north:
Quaint and Historic Forts of North America is a history and travel book by John Martin Hammond, published in 1915 by Lippincott. Hammond had written before on the old houses of Maryland and Delaware. Seventy-one illustrations go with the text. The book opens with a survey called Strongholds of the Past. Then it tours the forts one by one. Fort Independence in Boston Harbor comes first. Fort Columbus on Governor's Island follows.

The tour runs north to Ticonderoga and Crown Point on Lake Champlain. Quebec and Halifax get chapters of their own. Castine and Pemaquid in Maine, Niagara, and Oswego take the tale west. Mackinac Island and Fort Massac on the Ohio stand near the far end. West Point has its own place in the list. The book mixes war tales with notes on what a traveller may still see.
54954-oscar-in-africa:
Oscar in Africa is a boys' adventure novel by Harry Castlemon, copyrighted in 1882 and issued by the John C Winston Company of Philadelphia. Castlemon wrote the Gunboat Series, the Rocky Mountain Series, and the War Series. A frontispiece shows Oscar's narrow escape. The chapters promise a full safari of incident.

An inquisitive landlord and African treachery open the book at home and abroad. A disgusted sportsman and an English Nimrod supply the hunting party's colour. Oscar completes his outfit, baffles a swindler, and at last reaches his hunting grounds. A fight and a retreat, a midnight alarm, and a cowardly after-rider fill the African chapters. Castlemon was among the most popular American boys' writers of his century. His Oscar books sent young heroes round the world with rifle, camera, and pluck.
55400-common-cause-a-novel-of-the-war-in:
Common Cause, a novel of the war in America by Samuel Hopkins Adams, came out in 1919. Houghton Mifflin published it in Boston and New York. Arthur William Brown drew the illustrations. The story opens in 1912, in the American city of Fenchester. Three thousand voices fill the Fenchester Auditorium. They are singing Deutschland über alles at a German societies' convention.

Young Jeremy Robson of The Record reports the scene. His neighbour Galpin of The Guardian names the notables on the stage. Governors, brewers, pastors, and ward bosses fill the platform. Adams wrote the novel as America came out of the Great War. Its subject is the pull of the old country on German-Americans. Loyalty, propaganda, and belonging drive the plot. The opening chorus, sung in peace, sounds very different once the reader knows the war is coming.
56321-a-tour-through-south-america:
A Tour Through South America is a travel book by Forrest, with one hundred forty five pictures by the author. Stanley Paul published the work at London in 1913. Forrest dedicates the book to a shipping magnate famed on the South American routes. The contents run from the isthmus of Panama to the coffee lands of Brazil.

Early chapters treat the first adventurers, the sighting of the Pacific, and the buccaneers. Panama and its canal schemes take a large share. The road then runs through Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru, the country of marvels. Chile's nitrate fields, the Argentine camp, and Paraguay under its dictators follow. Rio, Sao Paulo, and the great forest close the survey. Forrest writes as a working artist travelling with his sketchbook.
56348-from-dublin-to-chicago-some-notes-:
George Birmingham wrote From Dublin to Chicago, some notes on a tour in America, printed in New York, copyright 1914. Birmingham had written Spanish Gold and General John Regan. Contents open with the spirit of adventure. Pressmen and public men follow. The hustling legend and holiday fever come next.

The iron trail, and forward, Chicago, lead on. A Memphis chapter and the land of the free fill the middle. Woman in the States and men and husbands stand in the list. The open door, colleges and students, and the Irishman abroad close the book. The first chapter opens on the title phrase itself. It may stand, Birmingham writes, as the sum of a tragedy: the long, slow flight of the Irish people from their own country. The younger men and women of the race flee the land of their birth for the new island of promise across the Atlantic.
5655-burke-s-speech-on-conciliation-with:
Edmund Burke delivered his Speech on Conciliation with America in Parliament in 1775, urging Britain to reconcile with its American colonies rather than coerce them. This school edition, edited with introduction and notes by Sidney Carleton Newsom, a teacher of English in Indianapolis, supplies background for students without a well-stocked library or time for collateral reading.

The editor draws sources listed under Bibliography to explain Burke's argument, his audience, and the crisis. Readers get one of the great parliamentary speeches, with student-friendly notes, arguing that conciliation serves empire better than force.
56829-peeps-at-many-lands-corsica:
Peeps at Many Lands: Corsica, by Ernest Young, came out in 1909. Black published the volume in London. Young was head master of a school at Harrow. Norbury painted the twelve colour plates. The series ran to some thirty lands, each in the same style. A general view of Ajaccio fronts the book. Seventeen chapters make the peep. History comes second, after a first look at the island. Aleria, Bonifacio, Calvi, and Bastia get chapters of their own. Ajaccio is joined with Napoleon, and Corte with Paoli.

The vendetta, the bush and forest, and a king of the bandits follow. Animals, character, and local legends close the book. Chapter one sizes the island: from its highest point, almost all of it can be seen. It is about three times the size of Yorkshire. Granite waves, Young calls its hills.
56853-journal-of-a-cavalry-officer-inclu:
Humbley, captain in the 9th Queen's Royal Lancers and a fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge, kept this Journal of a Cavalry Officer, published by Longman of London in 1854. The subtitle names its core: the memorable Sikh campaign of 1845 and 1846. A route map from Calcutta to the North West Provinces faces the title page.

The contents begin with the voyage to India and the march up country: Cawnpore to Meerut, then toward Ferozepore as war brewed. Cantonment life fills the middle: the cattle a march required, and the division of prize money. Suspicions of the Sikhs harden into chapters on the Sikh army. The battle of Moodkee opens the campaign. Humbley writes as a serving officer with a scholar's habits, noting roads, rations, and regiments alike. Military readers get the first Sikh war from the saddle.
56864-captain-billy-s-whiz-bang-vol-2-no:
Captain Billy's Whiz Bang, volume two, number seventeen, for February 1921, is a monthly humour magazine published by Fawcett at Robbinsdale, Minnesota. It cost twenty-five cents, and its motto is Make It Snappy. The editor, Captain Billy, was a Spanish and World War veteran, and the magazine is dedicated to the fighting forces of the United States. A Roosevelt quotation heads the masthead: we have room for but one soul loyalty, and that is loyalty to the American people.

The editor's column, Drippings from the Fawcett, opens with Prohibition thirst. About the first of September last year, Captain Billy writes, my cellar supply gave out. His old Turk friend Casey shanghaied him, cockeyed on a mixture he describes with relish. The Whiz Bang was the joke book of the doughboy generation, snappy, rural and irreverent.
56999-jack-chanty-a-story-of-athabasca:
Hulbert Footner wrote this northern adventure, published by Doubleday in 1913. A frontispiece shows Jack Chanty sprawling on his little raft in the wilds. The contents open with a hair-cut, then a company arriving from 'outside' and talk by the fire in the Athabasca country.

A conjuror, hearsay about Jack himself and the price of sleep follow in the chapters. Yellow metal, a showdown and a retreat lead into bear's flesh and berries for food. Tepees of the Sapis, an escape and an old score close a tale of rivers, hunger and hard travel in Canada's north.
57005-the-history-of-the-pyrates-vol-ii-:
Volume two of The History of the Pyrates, attributed to Captain Charles Johnson, gives the lives of fourteen pirate captains and their crews. The names run from Captain Misson and Captain Kidd to Captain Tew, Captain Bellamy, and Captain Condent. A map of the middle part of America opens the book.

Mixed into the lives is a description of Magadoxa in Ethiopia, with its laws, manners, customs, government, and religion. The appendix completes lives from the first volume and corrects mistakes. It adds the trial and execution of the pyrates at Providence under Governor Rogers. The title page says the matter was collected from journals of pirates and of commanders who fell into their hands. The History remains the great source book of pirate legend, half record and half romance.
57610-a-literary-historical-atlas-of-ame:
A Literary and Historical Atlas of America is a reference volume in Everyman's Library, edited by Ernest Rhys. Bartholomew compiled the atlas, which Dent published in London and Dutton in New York. It pairs coloured maps with the history and literature of North and South America.

The map list begins before Columbus. It opens with the Atlantic as Toscanelli drew it in 1474, then the discoveries of Columbus and of the Norsemen. Maps follow America from 1492 to 1522 and from 1522 to 1700. The United States is tracked in 1791, 1801 and 1845, and through the Civil War of 1861 to 1865. Cortes in Mexico in 1519 has a map, and the West Indies appear in 1650, 1763 and 1855. Such atlases let a reader of history or travel keep one finger on the map at all times.
57624-in-savage-africa:
In Savage Africa is a boys' adventure novel by Verney Lovett Cameron, a Royal Navy commander and African explorer. Its subtitle gives the hero's path: the adventure of Frank Baldwin from the Gold Coast to Zanzibar. The book was published in London in 1887 by Thomas Nelson and Sons, with thirty-two pictures. Cameron also wrote Across Africa, an account of his own crossing of the continent.

The chapter list promises a full tale of peril: leaving school, robbery and desertion, capture, and escape from a slave ship. Frank lives among native peoples and meets fetish men on his way. The story draws on Cameron's real knowledge of Africa in the age of the slave trade he fought against.
5794-rosa-alchemica:
Yeats opens Rosa Alchemica with an epigraph from Euripides blessing the one who knows the mysteries of the gods and purifies the soul through holy rites. The narrator then recalls meeting, for the last time more than ten years earlier, a figure who drew him toward secret orders, alchemy, and the pursuit of spiritual beauty. The tale that follows blends occult longing with lyric prose.

Readers meet Yeats in his symbolist phase, where roses, rites, and hidden masters stand for art itself. The story is short, strange, and richly written, favoring atmosphere over plain plot. It suits readers of Yeats, fin-de-siecle fantasy, and stories about artists tempted by magic, and it rewards those who enjoy prose that works like poetry.
58121-imperialism-in-south-africa:
Imperialism in South Africa is a pamphlet by Ewing Ritchie on the Transvaal. James Clarke of Fleet Street, London, put it out in the year 1879. The sixpenny pamphlet takes the annexation of the Transvaal as its head. Ritchie opens on the Puritan fathers and their resolving ways of old. They resolved the earth was the Lord's and the heritage of the saints.

Being themselves the saints, they took the natives' grounds as their own. That English faculty of appropriation made England mistress of the seas, he says. The British flag stands planted in every quarter of the globe thereby. India, Canada, the West Indies, Australia, and New Zealand gain by rule. Yet in some cases England has acted unjustly, Ritchie owns frankly. Money spent by millions was not unproductive, he argues in defence. Pride in countrymen's deeds should not blind the review, he holds.
59307-the-april-baby-s-book-of-tunes-wit:
A children's song book by the author of Elizabeth and Her German Garden. Macmillan published it at New York and London in 1900. Kate Greenaway drew the illustrations. The tunes are nursery rhymes with new music. Polly Flinders, Miss Muffet, and Jack and Jill all appear. A story explains how the tunes came to be written.

Three little sisters open that story, called April, May, and June. Their mother named them for their birth months. An aunt had wanted the eldest called Ophelia instead. Jane seemed too plain, and Ophelia too grand. The month names settled the family argument neatly. The sisters grew, and their doings generated songs. Greenaway's pictures made the volume a gift-book favourite.
59512-in-the-wilds-of-south-america:
Leo Miller of the American Museum of Natural History wrote of six years of exploration in South America, printed in New York in 1919. Over seventy illustrations and a map fill the book, which Miller gives to his wife. A painting by Fuertes shows the cock of the rock at home. The voyage from Panama to Buenaventura opens the tale.

Part one covers Colombia, from Cali and the Cauca Valley to Popayan and the Choco coast. A quest for the cock of the rock gives one chapter its aim. Later parts cross Venezuela, British Guiana, Peru, Bolivia, Argentina, Paraguay, and Brazil. Birds and beasts, rivers and high paramos fill a naturalist's field record of rare lands.
59662-the-coal-measures-amphibia-of-nort:
The Coal Measures Amphibia of North America, by Roy Lee Moodie of the University of Illinois, was put out by the Carnegie Institution of Washington in 1916 as its Publication Number 238. The first note sets its place in a chain of deep-time studies. Case had mapped the backboned beasts of the Permo-Carboniferous rocks in four books and summed their world in a fifth. Moodie's work fills the age just before: the frog kin of the coal swamps.

The note argues that rock lore and life lore must be read as one, and that no lone man can hold both. The Carnegie plan, with its staff free to call on peers, made such joint work real. Fossil fans get a grave monograph on the first land beasts of the coal age, set in their lost world of land and sea.
59750-ulysses-of-ithaca:
Ulysses of Ithaca is a youth form of the Greek hero tale by Karl Friedrich Becker. George Upton turned the German work to English for this set. A Chicago house brought it out in a Life Stories set in nineteen twelve. Four cuts dress the book of roam and home wait. Becker wrote old world tales for German boys and girls in his day.

Those tales won great love and still hold it, the front note claims. Gods and heroes stand in them in plain human light and warmth. Penelope waits year on year while suitors crowd her hall with coarse pleas. Her son Telemachus sails for word of his sire at a god prompt. Cyclops, Circe, Calypso, and twin sea fiends crowd the roam path.
60060-with-poor-immigrants-to-america:
With Poor Immigrants to America is a travel book by Stephen Graham, out in September of nineteen fourteen. Graham was known for a past book of a trip with far pilgrims to a holy city. Past thirty plates from his own shots fill this book. Parts of it first ran in a great press sheet.

Parts trace the sea trip, the come of the new folk, and the road past the land by foot. Slavs at a coal town, a feast day of the land, the tongue of the land, and the dance of the races all take parts. The front plate shows the new folk in sight of the great green statue in the port of New York. Graham thanks hosts who showed him the land as she is.
60704-the-book-of-the-lover-and-the-belo:
A mystical classic by Ramon Lull, translated from the Catalan. E Allison Peers made the translation and wrote an introductory essay. The Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge published it at London in 1923. Lull lived in thirteenth-century Majorca, not long after Saint Francis. Peers calls him the apostle of Africa. His book is a dialogue of the lover and the beloved.

The average man misunderstands the mystic, Peers begins. Mystic life looks like indolence from outside. In truth it is ceaseless spiritual activity, restless toward union. Lull was no cloistered dreamer, the essay insists. Scholar, man of affairs, and missionary shared one life. He who loves not lives not, runs his famous phrase. The short dialogues that follow burn with that love.
61307-captain-billy-s-whiz-bang-vol-2-no:
Captain Billy's Whiz-Bang was a pocket humor magazine for ex-servicemen, and this is its September 1921 number. Volume two, number twenty-four, opens with advertisements aimed at veterans of the war. One offers the Stars and Stripes paper to men going back to Paris in memory, with a book of Wally's overseas cartoons.

Bathing beauties in real photographs are promised further on in the advertising pages. The Whiz-Bang itself mixed jokes, verse and cartoons of soldier life into a small, spicy monthly. Fawcett, its captain Billy, built a publishing empire on the doughboy humor that fills numbers like this one.
61818-on-being-negro-in-america:
J Saunders Redding wrote essays on being Negro in America, published in 1951, opening with a French visitor's remark: what a self conscious people your Negroes are. He was right, Redding answers. The Negro lives constantly on two planes of awareness. Watching Ezzard Charles, the Negro heavyweight champion, fight a white challenger, a friend confessed he disliked Charles yet had to root for him.

One's heart is sickened, Redding writes, at the energy spent on the sheer business of living as a Negro. His other books are listed: To Make a Poet Black, They Came in Chains, and An American in India. Redding taught at Hampton Institute.
61864-captain-billy-s-whiz-bang-vol-3-no: Captain Billy's Whiz Bang, volume three, number twenty-seven, for November 1921, is the famed joke monthly put out at Robbinsdale, Minnesota, by W H Fawcett. The front pages are the sworn claim the law asks of such a sheet: names of owner and staff, set down for the Post Office. Harvey Fawcett swears to the list. No number twenty-six stands in the run; the count jumps from twenty-five to this one.
62077-captain-billy-s-whiz-bang-vol-3-no:
A humour monthly boasts in Captain Billy's Whiz Bang, volume 3, number 28, dated December 1921. The magazine comes from Robbinsdale, Minnesota, and claims a million and a half readers on its face. The number opens not with a joke but with a railway letter.

A Great Northern Railway officer writes from Saint Paul in September 1922. His train was held at Robbinsdale thirty seven minutes, loading what is stated to have been thirty six thousand pounds of mail. He asks the editor for the facts of publication: how often the magazine appears, on what dates, and the weight of each issue. With that word, he says, the road can make arrangements, perhaps a baggage car set out the day before. The letter tells the story, the editor crows. Had the winter annuals been loaded at one time, the Whiz Bang would have filled an entire mail train.
62287-the-collector-s-guide-no-17-januar:
The Collectors Guide number 17, for January 1940, is a monthly paper for people who buy and sell old books and prints. James Madison put it out from New York. A year cost two dollars, and one copy cost twenty five cents.

The paper serves fans of first printings, Americana, old papers, sheet music, playbills, and dime novels. Ads from New York shops fill many pages, with firms that buy autographs, rare books, and early American prints for cash. One shop seeks first printings by Kipling, Stevenson, and Twain. Book notes list new works for dealers and fans, with prices. The issue shows the trade in old print as a busy, cash ready world on the eve of war.
62832-outdoor-cooking-with-reynolds-wrap:
Reynolds Metals Company made a booklet on outdoor cooking with aluminum foil. Outdoor Cooking with Reynolds Wrap came from Richmond, Virginia, in 1950, priced at ten cents. The guide speaks to scouts, campers, picnickers, fishermen, and hunters. All methods and recipes were field-tested by known camping hands, it states.

Foil wraps mold to any shape and seal with a crimp, no strings needed. Campers drop wrapped meals in hot coals and skip scouring pots and pans. Foil ovens bake bread, biscuits, and small pies by the fire. Cooks gain dozens of proven ideas for tastier camp meals.
63012-south-america:
South America is the annual address of Gardiner Hubbard, president of the National Geographic Society, printed in the society's magazine in March 1891. Hubbard had given his earlier addresses on Africa, the dark continent, and Asia, the land of mountains and deserts. This year he chose South America, the land of rivers and pampas, he told the society in December 1890.

The recent Pan American Congress, he notes, has drawn attention to the southern continent. Its republics are rich in products the north lacks, while they buy their made goods from other lands. North and South America should be more closely united, he argues, for each completes the other. The address surveys the continent's great features: its long mountain chains, next to the Himalayas in height, running to the Panama isthmus and beyond. It is an early number of a magazine that would teach geography to millions.
63099-the-radio-boys-in-darkest-africa:
Gerald Breckenridge wrote a boys book printed at New York in 1923. Breckenridge had written The Radio Boys on the Mexican Border, with the Revenue Guards, and on Secret Service Duty. You certainly won his heart that time, Bob, a picture cries, look at his face for real amazement. Wimba's trial opens the tale.

Look here, Jack, we ought to do something to help Wimba, one boy says, I don't believe he's getting a square deal. Nor I, Frank, but what can we do, Jack Hampton answers, Chief Ruku Ru is supreme here. The party had engaged bearers at Nairobi, the capital of British East Africa, the text shows. Radio sets, Kikuyu country, and a friend on trial fill the road. Wireless was the wonder toy of the age, and Breckenridge marched it into every wild place.
64105-children-of-south-america:
Children of South America is a book for young readers by Katharine A Hodge, one of the Other Lands series from Oliphants. Eight illustrations in colour go with the text. A mapuche mother and baby stand at the front. The preface is dated November 1915. Its hope is plain: where there is darkness now, there may be knowledge and light. The chapters tour the continent by country, each with a playful name.

Brazilian Brownies and Blossom Babies open the run. Paraguayan Piccaninnies and Argentine All-Sorts follow. The small dwellers in the Land of Fire get a chapter of their own. Chilian Children, Bolivian Bairns, and Pearls of Peru close the list. Each chapter sketches the homes, dress, and ways of the children of its land. The book was made to widen a child's map of the world, and to stir care for missions abroad.
64241-other-worlds-a-story-concerning-th:
Other Worlds is a work of economic fiction by Lena Jane Fry, published by the author in Chicago in 1905. The subtitle states its argument. The story concerns the wealth earned by American citizens, and shows how it can be secured to them instead of to the trusts.

Twenty-seven chapters carry the tale, and a closing section describes a wealth producing and distributing society. A second story, set on the planet Venus, follows. The introduction reprints a newspaper piece asking whether a right to work exists. Fry presents herself as answering the cry for employment for willing hands. A portrait of the author fronts the volume. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
6445-letters-from-america:
Rupert Brooke started in May 1913 for the United States, Canada, and the South Seas, returning at the beginning of June next year. The first thirteen chapters were written as letters to the Westminster Gazette. Henry James prefaces them, writing on how a true poet comes into his estate, asserts identity, and reaches readers as a poet despite accidents and dangers. Brooke would have written a longer travel book instead, but these letters stand as printed.

Arrival, New York, Boston and Harvard, Montreal and Ottawa, Quebec and the Saguenay follow, with Ontario, Niagara Falls, Winnipeg, prairies, and Rockies. A Broadway car runs along the island's backbone. Cross streets curve down to a mysterious evening sky of dull reds, yellows, amber, pale green, and pink flecks, with the sun's flushed, smoke veiled face. Brooke writes America as a poet traveller, bright eyed and homesick at once.
64520-thoughts-on-south-africa:
Thoughts on South Africa is a set of land pieces by Olive Schreiner. An Unwin house of London brought it out first in nineteen twenty three. She wrote Dreams, Trooper Peter Halket, and Woman and Labour in past years. She gives the pieces to her mate as stray thoughts on a loved land. They were writ at Hanover in Cape Colony in October of nineteen one.

Her front note says the rest were held back four years by the times. Men at the Cape then bent low to Boer feet for base ends, she writes. A kind English voice on Boers might be read as fawn speech then. She dwelt long with Boers, shared their days, and knew their tongue. Boer scene lore heads the set, drawn from a Fortnightly sheet piece.
6462-an-introduction-to-the-mortuary-cus:
Dr. H. C. Yarrow, acting assistant surgeon, United States Army, writes this Smithsonian Bureau of Ethnology introduction to mortuary customs among North American Indians, printed at Washington in 1880. Director J. W. Powell presents it as the third of a series to promote anthropologic research. The first, by Powell himself, covered Indian languages, and the second, by Colonel Garrick Mallery, covered sign language.

Further volumes in preparation, the letter promises, will cover medicine, music, and other subjects. A mid passage describes a cave near the Stanislaus River in Calaveras County. Skulls now in the Smithsonian collection were taken from it, two miles from Abbey's Ferry on the road to Vallicito. Yarrow writes a field manual, gathering burial customs systematically for researchers who follow.
64675-in-brightest-africa:
In Brightest Africa is a memoir of big game hunting and museum work by Carl Akeley. The Garden City publishers issued this memorial edition, from rights running 1920 to 1923. Akeley dedicates the book to the memory of Theodore Roosevelt. An old Arab saying stands below: he who has drunk of Africa's fountains will drink again.

The contents move from elephant friends and foes to lions, buffalo, and leopards. Later chapters treat the gorilla hunts in central Africa and climbs on high volcanoes. A closing chapter describes the Roosevelt African Hall as a record for the future. The first chapter tells how a farm boy near Clarendon, New York, took to birds. By sixteen he had declared himself a worker in the art of mounting animals. Maps and line drawings trace his routes through elephant and gorilla country.
64847-headhunters-of-nuamerica:
Stanton Coblentz wrote Headhunters of Nuamerica, a tale printed in a magazine of March 1941. It opens as Downey comes back to his senses, stunned and stiff. His head hammers, and his joints ache as if he had been drugged or sandbagged. He lies in darkness in a narrow gallery, with a faint light ahead. A low moan sounds just in front of him on the floor.

He feels his way and knows the slim form sprawled there: Judith Barclay. Memory leaps back over the last hour or two of horror. War had been announced, and raiding planes came almost at once. He had appealed to Judith, who for the twentieth time shrugged and refused him. Then came the alarm, and their flight through panicky crowds. Coblentz drops his pair into a future war of raids and ruins.
64970-valladolid-oviedo-segovia-zamora-a:
Valladolid, Oviedo, Segovia, Zamora, Avila, and Zaragoza describes six Spanish cities in one volume. Calvert wrote the account. Lane published it in London and New York in 1908. The book belongs to a Spanish series that Calvert edited. Companion volumes treat Goya, Toledo, and Seville. No fewer than 413 illustrations crowd this one.

Six chapters divide the cities between them. Valladolid takes the longest share. Its museum's carved choir stalls fill plate after plate. The house where Columbus died is pictured. So is the palace where a Spanish king was born. Oviedo and Segovia follow in turn. Zamora and Avila come next. Zaragoza closes the survey at the end.
65244-on-criminal-abortion-in-america:
Horatio Storer, a Boston physician, published On Criminal Abortion in America with Lippincott in 1860, after the essays ran in a medical review through 1859. The treatise, part of a series on obstetric jurisprudence, argues that the law of his day largely ignored the unborn.

Storer sets the common law, which he says treated abortion mainly as an offence against the mother, against a moral law under which wilful killing at any stage of existence is murder. He holds that the offence, where common, concerns moralist, jurist, physician, and the whole community, and that its neglect shames both law and medicine. The dedication names his intended readers: physician, attorney, juror, judge, and parent. The book is a leading document of the nineteenth-century campaign by physicians for stricter abortion laws.
65502-faster-ways-to-favorite-dishes-wit:
Faster Ways to Favorite Dishes sells the new Minute Tapioca speed. The 1934 booklet promises lighter, more delicate tapioca desserts now. A tapioca cream as light as a whip heads the glad news. The new product cooks in five minutes once liquid scalds.

Old ways took fifteen minutes and far more dishes to wash. More than a dozen cream desserts fill the small recipe book. Fruit tapiocas for every season and baked puddings follow inside. Nineteen recipes use tapioca as a precision aid from soup to pie. A minute tapioca cream recipe opens the booklet as its best and easiest first.
66016-observation-on-the-use-and-abuse-o:
Observations on the Use and Abuse of Mercury is a med tract of note. Philips Wilson, a healer of two high guilds, wrote the tract. It came out in Winchester and London in the year 1805. Its aim is twofold, as its first words tell the lay reader.

False fears of the drug block its right use in sick folk, he says. Wild use of it, with no care, does much harm in its turn. That harm brings the drug a bad name it does not earn. He sets out what ills a wrong use brings and how they show. Then a man can tell those ills from ills of an other spring. No drug in the chest is prized more by healers, he holds. Its true fields are two: the hot swell and the blocked gland.
66206-frank-reade-jr-with-his-new-steam-:
Noname wrote a dime tale of Frank Reade Jr and his new Steam Man in Central America. Frank Tousey issued the tale from North Moore Street in New York. The Frank Reade Library cost 2 dollars and 50 cents a year by post. Frank, a famed maker of strange machines, reads a paper in his library at the start.

News says Tony Buckden, an old college friend, is lost in the Yucatan jungle. Six weeks of search found no trace of the young mining man. His rich father offers 50,000 dollars for proof of life and safe return. Frank weighs duty, his wife's fears, and the Steam Man's power for the rescue.
66329-what-the-negro-has-done-for-libert:
Professor John Moore of Boston published this pamphlet in 1895 under the title The Negro and American Liberty. He printed it himself in Boston, and a portrait of Crispus Attucks, the first to fall in the Boston Massacre, stands at the front. The question of the piece is what the Negro has done for liberty in America.

Moore opens with the paradox. A people brought here in chains, held as property, and shut out north and south from fair chances could hardly be expected to love the cause of freedom. Yet, he argues, the colored man showed an intense love of liberty, and a will to fight for the common cause even when his own share looked hopeless. He calls this a magnanimity never surpassed by any race. Readers get an 1895 case for a debt the country had not paid.
66398-the-gift-of-black-folk-the-negroes:
The Gift of Black Folk, the Negroes in the making of America, is a history by Du Bois, issued at Boston in 1924. Du Bois had written The Souls of Black Folk and edited a magazine of his race. An introduction by a white scholar frames the book. Its contents open with a foreword and a prescript, then turn to the gifts themselves.

Black explorers come first, then black labour, then black soldiers. The freeing of democracy and the rebuilding of freedom follow as chapters four and five. The freedom of womanhood, the American folk song, and Negro art and letters fill the later list. The gift of the spirit closes the book. Du Bois argues that America was made in part by black hands and black song, and that the nation owes its makers an honest accounting.
6693-people-of-africa:
Edith How's People of Africa, in its 1921 edition from the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge and Macmillan, surveys African peoples for young readers. The electronic edition notes two small slips fixed in the text: sandstorm misspelled on page twenty-one, and bought where brought was meant on page thirty-three. Such care shows the editor's wish for a clean text.

How writes as a missionary educator of her day, with a view of Africa shaped by her time and faith. Readers today will find both information and period attitudes in her pages. People of Africa is a useful historical record of how Africa was taught to English children a century ago.
67285-the-rover-boys-at-big-bear-lake-or:
Arthur M Winfield, the pen name of Edward Stratemeyer, wrote The Rover Boys at Big Bear Lake, or The Camps of the Rival Cadets. Grosset and Dunlap in New York issued the book, with pictures. A plate cries Bang, Crack, Bang as the boys guns go off. The book stands late in the long Rover Boys run. Lists in front name more than twenty earlier Rover tales and the Putnam Hall cadet books.

The Rover boys head for camp at Big Bear Lake, where rival cadets hold a camp of their own. School, camp, hunt, and lake sports shape the fun of the series. Stratemeyer built the tales for pace, jokes, and clean peril for boys. Readers meet old friends in a fresh wild setting, with contests on land and water. The book shows why the Rover name sold for decades to young America.
67333-the-native-races-of-british-north-:
Hambly surveys first peoples in The Native Races of British North America, printed for the Oxford University Press in 1920. Humphrey Milford issues the book across the empire's cities. Hambly held an Oxford diploma in anthropology, and had served as assistant anatomist in a research expedition to the Sudan. A chief's portrait and a tribal map illustrate the work.

Six chapters map the field. The country and its people lead, then some occupations of Indian tribes and social life among them. The social life of the Eskimo and the Eskimo as a hunter fill the northern span. Tales told by the Eskimo close the book. Chapter one starts with Columbus. The old world was startled in 1493 by the great navigator, it says. He called the native population Indians because he thought that sailing west he must come to India.
67656-south-west-africa:
William Eveleigh wrote South West Africa, issued by T Fisher Unwin in London, first published in nineteen fifteen. Eveleigh had earlier written A Short History of South African Methodism. He gave the book to General Botha. Eleven chapters fill the volume. Chapter one is The Land. The territory was formerly German South West Africa, the text notes, and is now British.

A glance at the map shows a triangular mass with its abrupt apex resting on the Orange River, Eveleigh says. Ovamboland in the north, Damaraland in the centre, and Great Namaqualand in the south divide the land. A tongue in the north east is called the Caprivizipfel. The whole area is three hundred twenty two thousand four hundred fifty square miles. Half a dozen Englands could drop into it with ease, he adds. Later chapters treat climate, flora, fauna, German occupation, the people, diamond fields, and the economic future.
68067-frank-reade-jr-with-his-new-steam-:
Frank Reade Junior, with his New Steam Horse in the Great American Desert, is a tale signed Noname. The Frank Reade Library sold by the year for two dollars and fifty cents, from Frank Tousey at New York. Frank Reade Junior is a famed young inventor in the tales.

His father was a famed inventor before him, and the son took to the trade by nature. The New Steam Man had caused a stir, but the Steam Horse beat it for skill. News of a desert trip with the horse roused wide public interest. The first chapter opens the case of Benjamin Astley. Speed, peril, and machine wonders drive the plot.
68276-slavery-and-the-slave-trade-in-afr:
Henry M Stanley lays out the facts in Slavery and the Slave Trade in Africa, an illustrated volume from Harper and Brothers in 1893. He quotes the Prince of Wales at the Antislavery Society's jubilee: spread true word of the trade's enormities, and show slave-holding states the gains of free labor. Stanley aims the same word at readers in America and England.

He promises the present state of Africa as to slavery, slave-raiding, and the trade, and the efforts to end them by opening the continent to honest commerce. Plates show a caravan's rear, a slave market, and captives taken.
68716-some-phases-of-educational-progres:
Walter Montgomery, a specialist in foreign school systems for the Bureau of Education, wrote this report for the Department of the Interior. It appeared as Bulletin 1919, Number 59, printed in Washington in 1920, and sold for 10 cents a copy. The pages began as advance sheets from the Biennial Survey of Education for 1916 to 1918.

Country by country, the report tracks how schools were changing across Latin America. Central America gets a section on trade and shop training, with notes on Guatemala, Salvador, Honduras, Costa Rica, Nicaragua, and Panama. Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Uruguay, and Venezuela each get their own survey. Counts of pupils who cannot read, teacher training, high schools, and trade schools fill the pages.
68800-angelica:
Elisabeth Sanxay Holding wrote Angelica, a novel published in New York by the George Doran Company in 1921. Her other novels, Rosaleen Among the Artists and Invincible Minnie, stand on the title page. The dedication hints at the theme: to a restless seeker for romance, this story of the end of a romance.

The book opens downstairs. Kennedy, janitress of a Harlem apartment house, gets up from her knees and wrings out the filthy cloth. She has just scrubbed the stairs. Pail in hand she descends to her basement flat: three black little rooms with barred windows on an air shaft, where ash cans stand and cats prowl. Roaches scatter over the wash tubs as she lights the gas. She lives rent free for the work, a good housewife in a place that fights her. Holding begins her romance in the basement.
68854-three-years-of-war-in-east-africa:
Three Years of War in East Africa, a campaign memoir by Captain Angus Buchanan, was first published by John Murray in July 1919 and reprinted in January 1920. Buchanan served in the East African campaign of the First World War. Maps and photographs from the field support the text.

Nine chapters run from the trip out to the end of the campaign on German soil. Frontier life, cattle raiders, and three stages of advance fill the middle of the book. A chapter of nature notes reflects his eye for wild life, formed in earlier years in Canada. A closing chapter looks past the war. The index ends the volume.
6886-first-footsteps-in-east-africa:
Richard Burton recounts his journey into East Africa and his exploration of Harar, a city then closed to most outsiders. He dedicates the book to James Grant Lumsden of Bombay, in whose house the plan for African travel had taken shape. A preface explains how the scheme began in May 1849, when the Royal Geographical Society sought leave to learn the resources of the Somali country.

Burton writes as a private traveler sent to test a land little known to Europeans, and he sets out the hopes, permissions, and risks that framed the trip. The narrative that follows traces his steps toward Harar, with notes on the people, routes, and towns along the way, in the plain style of a field report.
69162-hunters-three-sport-and-adventure-:
Thomas Knox wrote this tale of sport and adventure in South Africa. Dutton printed it in New York in 1895, Cary drew plates. A front plate shows a charging beast at page twenty nine. Chapter heads promise breakfast broken short by a big tusker chase.

A woman hunts elephants, Jack gets a hippopotamus, lions visit by night. Buffalo escapes, eland stalks, and a disputed prize fill mid chapters. Horse sickness, pitfall traps, and giraffe hunts follow in the field. Miss Boland kills a lion and stalks a giraffe in turn. Knox was known for the Boy Travellers books for youth.
69178-an-account-of-the-slave-trade-on-t:
An eyewitness account of the slave trade by Alexander Falconbridge. J Phillips printed it at London in 1788. Falconbridge had served as a surgeon in the African trade. He leaves the trade's general injustice to abler pens. His own aim is factual report. He tells what he saw himself. Trusted witnesses supply the rest. The story runs from capture in Africa to sale in the West Indies.

One theme sets the book apart. Falconbridge stresses the sufferings of the seamen. Climate, crowding, and harsh commanders killed them in numbers. Few writers had treated that subject with care. The book appeared as abolition pressure rose in Parliament. It became key first-hand testimony against the trade.
69757-dawn-in-darkest-africa:
Dawn in Darkest Africa is John H Harris's account of the Congo and its reform. Smith, Elder and Company published it in London in 1912. The Earl of Cromer wrote the introduction, with a map and illustrations to follow. A Bakuba prince of the upper Kasai fronts the book. Cromer begins by warning readers about missionary evidence.

Officials, Cromer says, should be sceptical of facts from philanthropic sources. Zeal can outrun discretion, and he names cases from his own knowledge. Yet the benefits of missionary work outweigh its errors. Nowhere were they more conspicuous than in the Congo. The Congo's administration, he writes, was a disgrace to civilised Europe. He cites Sir Reginald Wingate's estimate for the Soudan. Its population under the Mahdi fell from 8,525,000 to 1,870,500. Over 75 per cent died or were killed. The Congo's European ruler, Cromer charges, was little more merciful by percentage.
69766-the-training-of-teachers-in-the-un:
The Training of Teachers in the United States of America is a study by two British women. Amy Bramwell and Millicent Hughes wrote the reports from a tour of schools. A trust fund sent five scholars to view schools in America in eighteen ninety three. The book came out in London in the year eighteen ninety four.

Two of the five took the training of teachers as their sole task. They toured schools and colleges that made teachers for the states. Their aim was to learn what provision the land made for that work. Notes in the front thank the trust for funds and leave to print. British schools then sought fresh models for how to train their own staff.
69810-the-pronunciation-of-greek-accent-:
The Pronunciation of Greek, Accent and Quantity, is a philological inquiry by John Stuart Blackie. Blackie was professor of Greek in the University of Edinburgh. Sutherland and Knox published the book at Edinburgh in 1852. Mottoes on the title page gather the authorities. Thomas Fuller is quoted for the English practice: we Englishmen speak Greek so as to understand one another, which nobody else can.

Blackie argues the question of how Greek should be sounded in the schools and universities. The inquiry weighs the modern Greek pronunciation against the Erasmian system taught in the west. Boissonade is quoted wishing the modern Greek pronunciation received in all academies. Seyffarth holds that Erasmus himself, faced with such variety, would have left common use untouched and safe. Accent and quantity, the music of the language, stand at the center of the dispute.
70109-historic-jamaica:
Frank Cundall wrote this historic account of Jamaica and its past. The West India Committee printed it in London in 1915. Fifty two illustrations show scenes, Up Park Camp in 1840 among them. Cundall served as secretary and librarian of the Institute of Jamaica.

Contents list governors, speakers, chief justices, and agents at front. Port Royal takes chapter one, with forts, buccaneers, and Morgan. The earthquake of 1692, fire of 1703, and Rodney look out appear. Saint Catherine and Spanish Town fill the second chapter contents. A Montaigne line on places steeped in famed men fronts the history as its motto.
70345-a-constitutional-league-of-peace-i:
A Constitutional League of Peace in the Stone Age of America is a tract by Hewitt of the state desk for the lore of man. It was first a part of a great guilds year book for nineteen eighteen and was struck on its own in nineteen twenty. Its theme is the league of five tribes of the east wood lands and its plan of rule.

Those five tribes, in what is now the chief state of the east, set up a band with a plan built on peace, right, just acts, and power. They spoke tongues of one stock of the north. Past four years of world war, men now strive for a like league of lands, the tract notes. That old band meant to draw all tribes of men in in time, not as thralls but as free kin in the band.
70725-the-republic-of-costa-rica:
Gustavo Niederlein wrote a full report on the Republic of Costa Rica. Niederlein led the science arm of the Philadelphia Commercial Museum. The museum's seal heads the book in a plate. Its board held the state's chief and the town's mayor by right. Wide tables crowd the book and were split for this form.

Land, crops, trade, and folk of Costa Rica fill the report. Counts and lists ground each part in trade facts. The museum sought to grow trade twixt the two lands. Such books went to mills, shops, and schools as guides. Trade men get a small land drawn in hard, clear lines. Maps of fact, not of fancy, rule it.
70831-great-bands-of-america:
Great Bands of America is a music book for young readers by Alberta Powell Graham, printed by Nelson at New York in 1951. Kurt Werth drew the frontispiece. Graham dedicates the book to those who make music for the people. She also wrote Strike Up the Band and books on Columbus and the roads to the White House.

The contents start with military bands. The United States Marine Band leads, under Major Santelmann, then the Navy Band under Commander Brendler. The Army Band and the Army Air Forces Band follow. Concert bands take the second part, and the Salvation Army Band has its own section under Captain Holz. Merle Evans, called the Toscanini of the Big Top, brings the circus in. College and university bands, led by Illinois, close the march. The book is a parade in print.
70927-wanderings-in-north-africa:
Wanderings in North Africa, by James Hamilton, was published in London in 1856. A notice warns that the pages passed through the press while Hamilton was away in the East, which may explain a few wrong spellings of names. A front plate shows rock tombs in the necropolis of Cyrene. Chapters move from Malta to Benghazi and deep into Cyrenaica.

Hamilton describes Benghazi's look, people, diseases, government, antiquities, dress, and trade. Later chapters treat Arab horses, modes of travel, the ruins of Cyrene, its theatre, temples, and aqueduct, and talks with a bey at an Arab feast. Tomb robbing and splendid tombs draw his eye. The book is a keen, dated record of a little-known coast before modern travel.
70973-the-agricultural-and-forest-produc:
The Agricultural and Forest Products of British West Africa is a handbook by Gerald Dudgeon. Dudgeon had been Inspector of Agriculture for British West Africa. He later directed agriculture in Egypt. The book belongs to the Imperial Institute handbook series. Those handbooks cover the commercial resources of the tropics. Wyndham Dunstan, director of the Institute, edited the series. This is the second edition, published by John Murray in 1922.

A preface by Dunstan opens the volume. The preface to this edition notes a setback from the Great War. It also notes lessons that war taught about raw materials. Maps and illustrations support the survey in the text. The book treats the farm and forest wealth of the region. It was issued under the authority of the Secretary of State for the Colonies. Readers gain a period survey of crops, timber, and trade goods.
71018-the-natives-of-british-central-afr:
Werner's The Natives of British Central Africa, in the series The Native Races of the British Empire, was published by Constable in 1906 with thirty-two full-page plates. The frontispiece shows women carrying water-jars at Chiromo. A memorial leaf remembers J R W, lost at Elmina in August 1891. Eleven chapters move from land and peoples to language, stories, and rule.

The contents map the ground in detail. Early chapters treat geography, climate, and the tribes, with their marks, ear ornaments, and chipped teeth. Religion and magic fill two chapters: ancestor-worship, Mulungu, rain-making, charms, and witchcraft. Later chapters cover childhood, marriage, funerals, farming, ironwork, and the Bantu tongues. Kinship counted through women and the powers of the paramount chief close the survey.
7147-the-french-in-the-heart-of-america:
John Finley tells of the French in the heart of America from lectures first spoken in Paris. He gave them in the Sorbonne's Richelieu amphitheater, and in Lille, Nancy, Dijon, Lyons, Grenoble, Montpellier, Toulouse, Bordeaux, Poitiers, Rennes, and Caen. All stood in the American publisher's hands before the great war came, effacing with nearer adventures, perils, and anxieties the dim memories of French pioneers out in the Mississippi Valley.

Finley's purpose, as spoken, was to freshen and brighten for the French the memory of what some had seemingly wished to forget. He sought to visualize the vigorous, hopeful, achieving life passing before a background of Gallic venturing and praying. A simultaneous French publication was planned, less than a week before the undreamed of war broke. The book recalls France's lost American heartland.
71535-notes-taken-during-travels-in-afri:
John Davidson, a fellow of the Royal Society, kept these notes during travels in Africa, printed in London in 1839 for private circulation only. Davidson had died on the journey, and his brother put the pages out at the wish of friends who wanted a memorial of him. A front view shows Wadnoon from the roof of Sheik Beyrook's house, drawn from Davidson's own sketch.

The notes are rough and brief, the brother warns, penned at the moment under the most trying conditions. A sense of failure hangs over them, and the failure came true. Contents give the journal first, then loose papers, letters, and answers to queries. An appendix adds letters from Morocco, an account of his further progress in the desert, and an account of his death.
71649-french-enterprise-in-africa:
Hourst told his Niger voyage in French Enterprise in Africa, put in English by Mrs Arthur Bell. Chapman and Hall put it out at London in 1898, with 190 prints and a map. Hourst, a French naval officer, sailed the Niger from Timbuktu to the sea. The translator notes that no one had made that full trip before. She also warns that Hourst held a strong bias against England.

In spite of that bias, she calls his work good and of real worth. It adds much on the river, its basin, and the tribes on its banks. Most of all, Hourst kept the peace with local chiefs from start to Bussa. No life was lost on the whole trip, a rare feat on that route. The book gives travel, maps, and French aims in West Africa.
71970-the-jungle-folk-of-africa:
Robert Milligan's The Jungle Folk of Africa was published in 1908 by the Fleming Revell Company of New York, Chicago, and Toronto, a second edition at a dollar fifty. Press notices quoted at the front praise its grim fascination, and a companion volume, Fetish Folk of West Africa, is advertised beside it. A chief's canoe on the Cameron River illustrates the early pages.

The contents open with the voyage out: the change to the tropics, Sierra Leone, deck passengers, and Liberia. The coast follows, Old Calabar, Mount Cameroon, and a landing in the surf. Bush travel takes the reader where no white man had been, by caravan over African roads and bridges. Bush perils, with elephants and a caravan astray, and the camp-fire, with its legends of the snail and the chimpanzee, come after.
72480-the-fetish-folk-of-west-africa:
Robert H Milligan wrote The Fetish Folk of West Africa, a mission book on Gaboon peoples. Fleming H Revell Company issued it in New York, Chicago, and Toronto in nineteen hundred twelve. Milligan had written The Jungle Folk of Africa before. A Fang church teacher, Amvama, fronts the book in a plate.

The white man’s grave, that grim coast name, opens his tale. Quinine, coffins, and fright bred fever fill those first pages. Mpongwe and Fang folk then take the center of the book. King making, caste, house slavery, and witch trials crowd in. A tribe fades under rum ships and trade in one sad part. Fang looks, dress, food, and grim rites get a full study. Songs, dance, tales, and burial ways round out his close watch.
72488-industrial-and-commercial-south-am:
Annie S Peck wrote a survey of industrial and commercial South America, copyrighted in 1922. Peck had written a search for the apex of America and a South American tour guide. An opening chapter treats South America as a whole. Then the north coast is taken country by country, starting with Colombia.

For each land, chapters cover area, history, government, and population in turn. Physical features, the capital and chief cities, ports and transport, and resources and industries follow in fixed order. Venezuela and the Guianas complete the north coast section. Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia open the west coast section. The pattern suits traders and travelers needing compact facts.
73391-the-birds-of-jamaica:
Birds of Jamaica is a natural history by Philip Henry Gosse, aided by Richard Hill of Spanish Town. The London edition is dated eighteen forty seven. A companion book of illustrations is noted at the front. In his preface Gosse quotes White of Selborne on the pleasure of seeing the swallows of a hot and distant island. Very little is known of the habits of tropical animals, he writes.
