Nearly two hundred species of birds are ascertained to belong to the Jamaica fauna, he says. The knowledge comes entirely from original investigation, he stresses. Of several species he can give only rough indications, he owns. Many more have surely escaped the research of himself and his friends, he adds. A resident ornithologist's notes pervade the volume, and Gosse thanks him warmly.
73392-illustrations-of-the-birds-of-jama:
Illustrations of the Birds of Jamaica is a plate book by Philip Henry Gosse. John van Voorst of London issued the companion volume in eighteen forty nine. Gosse planned a figure for each species in his Birds of Jamaica work. Species well figured elsewhere and easy to find were later left out.

Plates keep the numbering of the species order in the main text book. Hawks, owls, nightjars, swifts, swallows, and todies open the plate list. Hummingbirds like the mango and polytmus species shine in the middle plates. Thrushes and other song birds follow in the ordered sequence given. Bound sets should follow the contents order, the notice directs.
73413-reynard-the-fox-in-south-africa:
Reynard the Fox in South Africa is a book of Khoikhoi fables and tales, translated by Bleek. Trubner published it in London in 1864. The tales were chiefly translated from original manuscripts. Those manuscripts lay in the library of Sir George Grey. The book belongs to children in South Africa and elsewhere, its dedication says. The contents sort the tales by their animal heroes. Jackal Fables open the collection in thirteen pieces.

The Lion's Defeat and The Lion's Share stand among those jackal tales. The White Man and the Snake and Cloud-Eating appear there too. Tortoise Fables and Baboon Fables form the next groups. The Judgment of the Baboon heads the baboon set. Lion Fables follow, with a flying lion among them. Bleek was a linguist recording oral tales in translation. The book preserves South African story telling in print.
73564-the-buccaneers-and-marooners-of-am:
The Buccaneers and Marooners of America is an account of the famous adventures and daring deeds of certain notorious freebooters of the Spanish Main. This new illustrated edition was edited by Howard Pyle and printed at London by Fisher Unwin in 1891. It stands in the Adventure Series with the lives of Trelawny, Robert Drury and John Shipp. Pyle's introduction and the translator's preface to the first edition open the book.

The first part, The Buccaneers of America, is the old buccaneer's own account. He sets forth for the western islands in the service of the West India Company of France and comes to the island of Tortuga. Then come the origins of the most famous pirates of the American coasts, with the exploit of Pierre le Grand. A front picture shows Morgan recruiting for the attack on Porto Bello.
73605-a-century-of-science-in-america:
Yale University issued a volume of its Silliman Memorial Lectures on a century of science in America. The lectures rest on a legacy of eighty thousand dollars left in 1883 in memory of Mrs Hepsa Ely Silliman. Her children gave the gift to Yale in New Haven. The fund came to Yale in 1901, and this book is the fourteenth volume of the series.

The lectures were meant to show the presence and wisdom of God in the natural and moral world. Yet the founder barred dogmatic theology and chose natural science and history instead. Astronomy, chemistry, geology, and anatomy got special weight. Past volumes tell of electricity, radioactivity, genetics, and solutions by famed hands.
73613-how-much-bolshevism-is-there-in-am:
How Much Bolshevism Is There in America gathers five pieces by Arno Dosch-Fleurot of The World. Press Publishing put the set out in New York in January 1921. Dosch-Fleurot had been the one United States news man in Petrograd when revolt broke out in March 1917. He stayed through the rule of Lenin and Trotsky to the fall of 1918. He then crossed the United States to test how much of that creed he could find at home.

One piece sets rich America by the side of poor, war-worn lands in Europe. One counts how much Bolshevism he found, and how much he did not. Later pieces look at unrest among workers and moves to form one big union for each trade field. The last shows how farm groups won gains that wage hands had not.
7390-the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendel:
Holmes was a doctor before he was a famous author, and this volume collects his medical poems. The Morning Visit opens on a sick man's chamber, where friendship must launch a sentiment though the patient cannot join the feast. The Two Armies, The Stethoscope Song, and a poem for the American Medical Association meeting of 1853 follow, with a comic Rip Van Winkle, M.D., among them.

The humor is a doctor's humor: leeches that bite, patients who become interesting cases, and the gap between textbook and bedside. Holmes jokes about his trade without ever scorning it, and the poems show why students loved his lectures. For readers of his essays, this volume is the verse companion to his medical life, light in touch and serious underneath.
74039-the-reader-s-guide-to-the-encyclop:
The Reader's Guide to the Encyclopaedia Britannica, a handbook of sixty-six courses of systematic study or occasional reading, was published in London and New York in 1913 by the Encyclopaedia Britannica Company. The courses point a reader to the articles in the encyclopaedia that serve a chosen line of work or study.

Part one gives courses for people in trades and callings. Farmers, stock-raisers, and dairy farmers come first, then merchants and manufacturers. Textiles, machinery, metals, furniture, and leather follow. Courses follow for insurance men, architects, builders, railroad men, engineers, printers, journalists, teachers, ministers, physicians, lawyers, bankers, and officers of the army and navy. Part two gives courses of reading to supplement school or university studies, from music and the fine arts onward.
74085-woman-s-work-in-america:
Annie Nathan Meyer edited a survey of the work of women in America, issued in New York in 1891 with a front essay by Julia Ward Howe. Meyer took the spark from a like book on the woman question in Europe. From the spring of 1888 she gathered facts and chose eighteen women to write the parts.

Each part takes one field of work, not one place, so the whole range of what women did can be seen at once. Meyer grants that some fields may seem too large or too small in the plan, but says no bias ruled her choice. The book stands as a stock taking of women's labor at a time of fast change in school, press, and trade.
74587-tropical-africa:
Tropical Africa is a travel and nature book by Henry Drummond of Scotland. John Alden of New York issued the American edition in eighteen ninety. Drummond also wrote Natural Law in the Spiritual World, a famed work. His portrait fronts this set of African lectures and diary pieces here.

Chapters open on the water route by the Zambesi and Shire rivers. The east African lake country of Shirwa and Nyassa follows in chapter two. The aspect and heart disease of Africa fill the middle chapters of it. Wanderings on the Nyassa Tanganyika plateau give a traveller diary in five. The white ant, mimicry in insects, geology, and a political warning close.
7526-the-englishwoman-in-america:
Isabella Lucy Bird, later famous for travels in Asia and the Rockies, made her first long journey in America, and this book records it. Andrew Hill Clark supplies foreword and notes. The voyage out opens the story, with practical joking, an unwelcome companion, American patriotism, and a first view of the new world, before the departure into the interior.

Halifax and the Blue Noses follow, with heat, disappointed expectations, coaches that were not what they seemed, and roads full of annoyances. Bird notes politics, chemistry, mathematics, rotten bridges, midnight arrivals, and Yankee conceit with a sharp, amused eye. The Englishwoman in America is a classic of Victorian travel writing: candid, curious, and never dull.
75580-affairs-of-west-africa:
Edmund D. Morel wrote this study of the state of West Africa, printed at London in 1902. He was a member of the West African part of the Liverpool Chamber of Commerce. Mary Kingsley wrote the word at the front of the book. The list of parts shows the plan of the work. The first part treats of five years of British trade with the west coast, of the old ways and the new, and of reforms the author holds to be of need.

The bulk of the book is Nigeria. Parts treat of the find of the north of that land, of the Hausas and their great mart, and of the chief trade of the south. More parts treat of rule, of funds, of the men of the faith of Islam, and of raids for slaves.
75773-two-years-captivity-in-german-east:
Two Years' Captivity in German East Africa gives the war experiences of a Royal Navy surgeon. His name is cut to initials on the title page of the London edition. Hutchinson published the book, and twenty chapters tell the whole of his captivity. The contents run from the loom of war to home at last.

The tale opens in a Portsmouth mess in the last days of July nineteen fourteen. The surgeon joins the battleship Goliath at Devonport as war breaks out. Treachery and capture follow in tropic seas in the early chapters here. Prison camps at Kilimatinde and Tabora, typhoid, and escape attempts fill the middle. A nightmare camp, release, and the voyage home close the two years. German cruelty to the native people is charged in one full chapter.
75833-fairy-tales-from-south-africa:
Fairy Tales from South Africa is a set of tales collected by Bourhill and Drake, published in 1908. Macmillan issued the book in London from Saint Martin Street that year. Holloway drew the illustrations for the volume of tales. It is addressed to all children who still love fairy tales in its dedication.

The collectors say the stories are real fairy tales, as much as Jack the Giant Killer or The Sleeping Beauty. They are traditional, handed down by word of mouth, in their account of the tales. Children sit round the fire at night and hear them from their grandmothers in those homes. The book is an early attempt to carry the oral tales of South Africa into English print for children, with the tellers terms of trust stated in its first pages.
76272-the-five-republics-of-central-amer:
The Five Republics of Central America is Dana Munro's thesis for the University of Pennsylvania, on the republics' political and economic development and their relations with the United States. Oxford University Press published it in 1918, under a Carnegie Endowment copyright.

Munro's preface answers a common American picture of the isthmus. Central America, he says, is conceived chiefly as a land of revolutions and bankrupt governments. Against it he sets the people's progress since independence, rarely recognised. He stresses the handicaps left by Spanish colonial rule. Three centuries of restricted intercourse and foreign officialdom stunted advance. Independence then found no experience of self-government and no institutions to build on. Some republics, he argues, have advanced despite it, and deserve a fairer judgment.
76281-the-wanderer-in-africa:
The writer known as ALOE wrote a tale showing forth the thirty second Psalm, printed at London and Edinburgh. She had written The Claremont Tales, Ned Franks, and Sheer Off. A full moon falls on a large black poisonous snake gliding over the sand in the front picture. Night on the waste opens the tale, then wanderings, forsaken, and not forsaken.

Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered, the Psalm heads chapter one. No use, it won't do, Hans Kuhe the Dutch Boer cries. Rhinoceros hide won't get another yard out of them beasts, and the wagon must outspan for the night. Pollux his driver had belaboured eight oxen for an hour in the sand. Peril at hand, resolutions, guidance, the stubborn sinner, and home close a desert lesson book for the young.
76940-the-narrative-of-an-explorer-in-tr:
The Narrative of an Explorer in Tropical South Africa is a travel book by Francis Galton, printed at London by John Murray in 1853. It has coloured maps, plates and woodcuts. A front picture shows a native group of Damaras and Ovampo. In his preface Galton says the pages describe a part of Africa hitherto unknown to Europeans, which he had lately travelled over and explored.

Its result was to fill up a blank in the maps. The country of the Damaras was explored first: warlike, pastoral blacks. Beyond them lay a broad tract of aboriginal Hottentots. On the return south, Galton proved that a workable route ran between the lake and the Atlantic. He also points to Ovampo-land as a fine opening for mission work.
77000-china-collecting-in-america:
Alice Morse Earle wrote China Collecting in America, copyrighted in 1892 and printed at New York with many illustrations. Earle gives the book to her sister Frances Clary Morse, the companion of her china hunts. The first chapter is China Hunting itself. Trencher, treen, and bright pewter come next, then the early use and bringing in of china in America.

Chapters follow on the earliest pottery wares, English porcelains in America, and Liverpool printed ware. Oriental china, the cosey teapot, and punch-bowls have their own heads. George and Martha Washington's china and the china of the presidents fill two more. Designs tied to Washington, Franklin, and Lafayette, and Staffordshire wares, close a guide made for hunters of old American china.
77303-a-tour-through-north-america:
A Tour Through North America, by Patrick Shirreff, was printed at Edinburgh in 1835. Shirreff was a farmer of Mungoswells in East Lothian. His book adds a full view of the Canadas and the United States, framed for folk who might farm abroad.

Shirreff clears up a rumor at the start, that East Lothian farmers sent him out to report. In truth his younger brother wished to try his luck as an American farmer. Shirreff crossed the sea to judge the step with his own eyes. He gives the book to John Deans, who saw many of the same scenes. Farm readers of 1835 got soil, prices, and ways of life from a plain man of the plough.
77411-the-country-seats-of-the-united-st:
William Birch made a plate book of the fine country seats of the United States. Birch was a painter in enamel who dwelt near Bristol, Pennsylvania. The book was planned and put out by Birch in 1808. Its rights were filed in January 1809 in Pennsylvania. A view of the Capitol at Washington heads the plates.

Seats of rich men stand in fine grounds through the book. Scenes tied to those seats add life to the views. Each plate shows a house as its age prized it most. Birch's own hand cut and colored the work with care. Past and art fans get a rare glimpse of young America. Few such plate books came from that shore then.
77511-travel-letters-from-new-zealand-au:
Travel Letters from New Zealand, Australia and Africa is a book of dated letters by Howe, published at Topeka, Kansas, in 1913. The form is the traveller's journal. Each entry is headed with its day, and the whole records a voyage round the southern world.

The first letter is written in the Pacific Ocean on Saturday, January 4, 1913. Howe is two days out of Sydney aboard the ship Sonoma, after seventeen days at sea. The passengers and servants already feel like old acquaintances. The voyage from San Francisco had some boisterous weather at first. The ship stopped eight hours at Honolulu and five at Pago Pago in Samoa. Christmas Day on board brought a big dinner, speeches, and a dance. New Year was kept the same way, though crossing the date line meant the travellers had no New Year's Day that year.
77558-black-america:
Black America is a study of the freed slave and his late master by W. Laird Clowes, out in eighteen ninety-one. Clowes was sent by a great London sheet in the fall of eighteen ninety to the south of the United States. His ten notes ran in that sheet past three months. The book prints them with large fresh parts and fixes.

Parts treat the black belt, the freed man as master and as he is, and the place of the south white. Late parts weigh plans to mend the state of things and name one best plan. Back parts give counts of folk, notes on caste, and the growth of the race. Clowes spoke with men of all sides and hues for the work.
78119-humanism-and-america:
Humanism and America holds essays on the fate of the modern age. Norman Foerster picked and shaped the set of talks for the book. Rights date the work to the year nineteen thirty. A verse on life as a long head ache in a loud street heads the front.

The front talk says all now live on the main street, not the side lane. Faith, grace, beauty, and trust in the crowd have all lost their pull. Doubt and revolt have in turn gone stale as cures for the age. The essays plead for a new creed of man at the core of life. Keen staff of great schools lend their pens to the joint plea.
78613-cacaos-and-chocolates-in-the-unite:
Cacaos and Chocolates in the United States of America, by Professor Nemo of Paris, was copyrighted in 1885. Huyler's Chocolate Works issued it from the corner of Eighteenth Street and Irving Place, New York. Its motto runs: health is better than wealth. Plates show the cacao fruit whole, cut lengthwise and across, the bean with and without its shell, and the blossom.

The preface holds that Americans know little of the properties of good chocolate and the benefits of its generous use as food and bon-bons. The book answers with a full account of manufacture. It traces the cacao bean from its growth to its final change into chocolate. It adds the decided opinions of eminent authorities of this country and of Europe, where chocolate has been longer and more abundantly used.
79104-historic-buildings-of-america:
Esther Singleton collected and edited Historic Buildings of America, As Seen and Described by Famous Writers, issued at New York in 1906 by Dodd, Mead and Company. Front pages list Singleton's books on towers, pictures, castles, and famous women. All follow one plan, great writers on great themes. A print of the Capitol at Washington heads the work.

The Capitol leads the contents with a piece by Joseph B Varnum. Charles Dickens writes on life within the Capitol. Arlington in Virginia is treated by Iza Duffus Hardy. Carpenters Hall is treated by Benson J Lossing. The Cradock House at Medford and Fraunces Tavern follow. William and Mary College closes the part shown here. Many pictures aid the tales of famed American buildings.
8159-wanderings-in-south-america:
Charles Waterton offered his Wanderings in South America with a hesitating hand, expecting jostles from critics and perhaps a fall in the field of modern criticism. His hope was modest: that some accidental rover, turning his pages, might imbibe the idea of exploring Guiana and giving the world an enlarged description of that noble country. Waterton's wanderings took him through Guiana's forests and rivers in search of natural history.

The book mixes travel, zoology, and personal adventure, with Waterton's eccentric energy on every page. He describes birds, beasts, and the hardships of tropical travel with the enthusiasm of a naturalist. As an early account of Guiana, it remains lively and influential, and a classic of English travel writing.
a-handbook-of-the-boer-war-with-general-: This anonymous handbook of the Boer War maps the conflict with a general map and eighteen sketch maps. Its chapters open with prolegomena on patriotism, duty, and discipline, then treat the Natal wedge and Kimberley. Ladysmith at bay, Mafeking, and the march from Bloemfontein to Pretoria follow. The handbook gives a clear campaign narrative for general readers.
a-start-in-life-a-journey-across-america: Charles Finch Dowsett promises a start in life in this guide to a journey across America and fruit farming in California, priced at one shilling. The contents run from London to Chicago, Chicago to San Francisco, and San Francisco to New Orleans. They then turn to California information: Merced land, prices, surveys, raisin culture, irrigation, and olive culture. Plans, maps, views, and samples of fruit and soil awaited readers at the firm's Lincoln's Inn Fields office.
a-winter-tour-in-south-africa: Frederick Young makes a winter tour in South Africa in this 1890 volume, printed again from the Royal Colonial Institute's Proceedings, with big extras, pictures, and a map. Dedicated by leave to Princess Louise, Marchioness of Lorne, the tour crosses a large part of Her Majesty's grand lands in South Africa. A picture of his wagon opens a foreword on settlements whose growth the author calls strange and fast.
a-yellow-god-an-idol-of-africa:
H. Rider Haggard opens in a magnificent City of London office built of Aberdeen granite, seat of Sahara Limited, a scheme to water the desert and enrich its promoters. Sir Robert Aylward, baronet and member of Parliament, runs the company. His nephew Alan Vernon, an engineer with a conscience, breaks with the scheme and with his uncle.

The contents promise the yellow god itself, a golden idol of the Asiki people, Jeekie's tale, dwarf folk, a hall of the dead, and a gold house. Alan sails for West Africa to return the idol his uncle's agents stole. Haggard mixes City fraud with African adventure, and the idol's curse hangs over both worlds.
academica: Marcus Tullius Cicero's Academica appears here in James Reid's revised text with explanations, published by Macmillan in 1874. The preface notes that Davies's edition of 1725 was the last by an English scholar, while Goerenz's German edition of 1810 proved poor and untrustworthy against Madvig's evidence. Davies remained superior but deficient by present standards of criticism, and Reid's notes grew from his Intercollegiate lectures at Christ's College.
an-englishman-s-travels-in-america: John Benwell travels as an Englishman in America, prefacing his account with the Englishman in America and chapters on the parts of the Union he visited. The book records American manners, towns, and institutions through a visitor's eyes. Benwell's plain observations give a useful picture of the young republic. His notes still help us see the early republic afresh.
an-introduction-to-the-mortuary-customs-:
Dr. H. C. Yarrow prepared this study for the Smithsonian Institution's Bureau of Ethnology, printed by the Government Printing Office at Washington in 1880, as the title page states. Director J. W. Powell's letter notes it is the third of a series meant to promote research among the North American Indians. Yarrow gathers reports on how the many peoples of the continent treated their dead.

The study sorts the customs by kind: burial in graves and mounds, scaffold and tree burial, cremation, and mummifying, with the mourning rites, feasts, and beliefs that went with each. Reports come from army officers, agents, and travelers across the continent. Yarrow's compilation, written in the terms of its time, preserves records of practices then fast disappearing.
bandelier-islands-titicaca:
Lake Titicaca and its sacred islands drew Bandelier south for his 1910 report. The Islands of Titicaca and Koati records his survey of the famed sites. In Inca belief, the sun itself was born on those shores.

Bandelier gives the shrines their first study with true care for method. He maps ruins, tests old claims, and weighs local lore with respect. The high lake, its boats, and its stone remains fill his notes. His fieldwork helped launch a real science of the Andes. Readers meet bold claims checked, at last, against stone and soil in the field. The report rewards slow, close reading.
britannica-1911-abaca: Abaca, also spelled Abaka, is the headword of a very short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry gives the word as a native name for the plant Musa textilis. That plant yields the fibre known in trade as Manila hemp, and the entry sends the reader to the hemp article for the full account. Nothing more is stated: no place, use, or history stands in the notice. Plant and fibre share one name in commerce.
britannica-1911-alcobaca:
Alcobaca, a town of Portugal, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands in the district of Leiria, on the Alcoa and Baca rivers, from which it takes its name, and held 2,309 people in 1900. The town's own size is modest. Its interest lies almost wholly in one great building complex at its heart.

A Cistercian convent, partly turned into schools and barracks, dominates Alcobaca. Its monastic buildings form a square 725 feet across, crowned by a huge conical kitchen chimney. Founded in 1148 and finished in 1222, the house rivalled Europe's greatest abbeys in size and wealth. Tradition says 999 monks kept mass going without pause through the year. French troops burned part of it in 1810, and it was secularised in 1834. The early Gothic church holds a fine cloister and the tombs of Peter I and Inez de Castro.
britannica-1911-alpaca:
Wool, not carrying power, is the alpaca's worth. Unlike the llama, it bears no loads; Indian blankets and ponchos are woven from its fleece. Flocks of alpacas graze all year on high Andean levels in southern Peru and northern Bolivia, fourteen to sixteen thousand feet up. The animal is one of two tamed breeds of South American camel kin, bred from the wild guanaco.

Trade then borrows the name twice over. Alpaca covers the animal's hair, and also a fabric style first made from it. Mohair, Iceland wool, and glossy English wools now serve as well. Four South American wool-bearers — llama, alpaca, guanaco, and vicuña — are set side by side. Cross-breeding trials are also reported, with offspring sold at Liverpool under a trade name, and readers are sent to the wool-manufacture entries for how the fibre is prepared and woven.
britannica-1911-angelica:
Britain knows the plant genus Angelica through a single wild species, A. sylvestris, a tall perennial herb of the carrot family. Large twice-divided leaves and broad clusters of white or purple flowers mark it. Gardeners loosely give the same name to Archangelica officinalis, a plant of a related genus whose tender shoots flavour aromatic sweetmeats.

Much of the entry turns to products drawn from the roots. Extracting them with alcohol, then ether, yields angelica balsam, holding angelica oil, angelica wax, and a substance called angelicin. The root oil carries a named terpene, and the seed oil adds two acids. A North American namesake closes the account: the angelica tree, a prickly Aralia species reaching eight to twelve feet, crowned by an umbrella-like head.
britannica-1911-athabasca:
Athabasca, also called Elk, is a river and lake of Alberta, Canada, and this 1911 Britannica entry gives their measures. The river rises in the Rocky Mountains near the Yellowhead Pass and flows north-east, then north, into Lake Athabasca. It runs 740 miles and takes in several large tributaries, among them the McLeod, the Pembina, and the Clearwater. The Lesser Slave river drains the lake of that name into it.

The lake itself runs 195 miles from west to east and covers 3,085 square miles, at 690 feet above the sea. It sends its waters north by the Slave river and the Mackenzie system to the Arctic Ocean. Its north shore is high and rocky, its south shore sandy and barren. Shallow-draught steamers work the lake and river, held up only at the Grand Rapids near the mouth of the Clearwater.
britannica-1911-bahia-blanca:
Bahia Blanca is a city and port of Argentina on the Naposta river, three miles from a deep, sheltered bay of the same name in the far south of Buenos Aires province. Its people numbered about 11,600 in 1903, and growth came as La Pampa and Neuquén opened to settlement inland.

The bay, among the best on the Argentine coast, makes the town the natural shipping port for those territories and the province's south, sending out great loads of wheat and wool. Argentina set its chief naval station here at Puerto Militar. Founded as a fort and trading post in 1828, the town took off only after its first railway in 1885. Brackish water and swamps made it unhealthy, a flaw a new supply from the Sauce Grande was meant to cure.
britannica-1911-beira-east-africa:
Beira is a seaport of Portuguese East Africa, and this 1911 Britannica entry describes the young port. It stands at the mouth of the Pungwe river, north of Delagoa Bay, with a railway running inland toward Cape Town. Its people number about four thousand, a third of them Europeans and some three hundred Indians. The town is built on a tongue of sand reaching into the river and is fairly healthy for its coast.

A masonry wall guards the sea front, and the port holds over thirteen thousand feet of wharfage. Ships drawing twenty-four feet can enter at high tide. The town has fine public gardens but no buildings of note. It is the headquarters of the Mozambique Company, which rules the Beira district under charter from the Portuguese crown.
britannica-1911-british-east-africa:
British East Africa, in its widest sense, covers all land under British sway on Africa's eastern side. German East Africa bounds it to the south. Abyssinia and the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan bound it to the north. It takes in the protectorates of Zanzibar, Uganda and East Africa.

Apart from a narrow coastal belt, the land belongs almost wholly to the great East African plateau. It rarely falls below 2000 feet. Broad sections rise to 6000 or 8000 feet. Steps and plateaus climb from the coast to high ground marked by strong traces of volcanic action, cut by the eastern rift valley with its lakes that have no outlet. Westward a lower basin holds Victoria Nyanza, drained north to the Nile, and beyond it the ground rises again to a second volcanic belt crowned by the Ruwenzori range.
britannica-1911-cajamarca:
Cajamarca is a city of northern Peru and head of its department. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives its height, churches, and dark fame. It sits in a high valley between two cordilleras. The town stands about ninety-four hundred feet above the sea.

Wide streets cross at right angles among low clay houses. An old parish church and a Franciscan house mark the town. Ruins of the palace of Atahualpa still stand there. Pizarro seized and killed that Inca ruler in this place in 1533. Hot sulphur springs east of town still draw bathers today. Wool and linen goods, leather, and metal work give trade. The city serves as a supply hub for a large inland region.
britannica-1911-cappello-bianca:
Bianca Cappello (1548–1587) became grand duchess of Tuscany. She was born into a rich and noble Venetian family. Her great beauty was famous from her youth. This 1911 Britannica entry tells her dramatic story. At fifteen she fell in love with Pietro Bonaventuri. He was a young Florentine clerk with the Salviati firm. On 28 November 1563 she fled with him to Florence. They married there, and she bore a daughter, Pellegrina.

Venice tried hard to have Bianca arrested and returned. The grand duke Cosimo protected the couple instead. Her husband's poor family set her to menial work. Then her beauty caught Francesco, the grand duke's son. He was married already, to the Archduchess Giovanna. He took Bianca as his mistress and showered her with gifts. Her husband found court work and other comforts. In 1572 he was murdered in a Florence street. The entry hints that the lovers may have known of the deed.
britannica-1911-caravaca:
Caravaca is a town of south-eastern Spain. It stands in the province of Murcia. It lies near the left bank of the river Caravaca. That river is a tributary of the Segura. Its population in 1900 was 15,846. This 1911 Britannica entry describes the town and its shrine. The medieval castle of Santa Cruz dominates the place. Several convents stand within the town as well.

The parish church at Caravaca is a fine building. It holds a cross famed for healing power. A yearly festival honours that cross on 3 May. Crowds gather for the feast in spring. The hills to the north are rich in minerals. Marble and iron are both found there in quantity. The town has no railway link at all. Still, it works as a real industrial centre. Large iron-works and tanneries operate in the town. Paper, chocolate and oil are also made there.
britannica-1911-casablanca:
Casablanca is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a seaport on the Atlantic coast of Morocco, called Dar el Baida, “the white house,” in Arabic. It ranks third among the towns of the Moorish coast and serves as the wool and grain port for central Morocco. The roadstead has no bar or bad rocks but lies open to north west winds, and steamers anchor in five to six fathoms. Harbour works begun in May 1907 promised shelter at all tides.

Foreign trade through the port ran at about £750,000 a year across the decade 1897 to 1907. A railway to Ber Reshid opened in September 1908, the first railway built in Morocco. About 20,000 people lived in the town, among them many foreign merchants and a consular corps. The entry also recalls the Portuguese past: they built on the site of Anfa, a town they had destroyed in 1468, and later abandoned the place.
britannica-1911-chuquisaca:
Chuquisaca is a department of southeastern Bolivia. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica splits it between plateau and plains. It lies high in the east and low toward the La Plata basin. Its area tops twenty-six thousand square miles.

The Pilcomayo River crosses its western part toward the Paraguay. Lowland air is hot, wet, and sickly for settlers. Plateau air is healthy but swings more in heat and rain. Wet months turn the east plains into great lagoons. Dry months parch those same plains into desert. Mines hold wealth but lag behind richer neighbor fields. Grazing rules the plains, with cattle, sheep, goats, and llamas. Grain grows in the rich valleys of the high ground. Pack animals haul all goods on three rough highways.
britannica-1911-cloaca: Cloaca was the Latin name for the sewers built to drain the low marshy ground between the hills of Rome, as a brief note in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica records. The chief of these drains, the Cloaca Maxima, emptied the forum. It dates from the sixth century before Christ. The drain ran ten feet six inches wide and fourteen feet high. Three rings of stone voussoirs formed its vault. Blocks of lava, cut in many sided shapes, paved its floor.
britannica-1911-confederate-states-of-am:
The Confederate States of America was the government formed by the seceding Southern states at the start of the American Civil War, in the winter of 1860 and 1861. Those states held roughly half the population of the North. In past national politics they had played a part past their share. Skilled statesmen, schooled in state politics and in Congress, framed the new union.

Jefferson Davis of Mississippi was the near-set choice for president. Alexander H. Stephens took the vice-presidency in his place. Stephens stood as a strong voice for states' rights. In war he became a sharp foe of Davis's use of power. Robert Toombs of Georgia, a strong secessionist, sat in the Confederate Congress. He too fought the grasping powers of the president. The long entry runs to war finance and home strain. Clever stand-ins for scarce goods, and fat profits from them, fill its middle pages.
britannica-1911-corsica:
Corsica is a large island of the Mediterranean sea and a French district. Its island entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies just north of Sardinia, split by the strait of Bonifacio. Counts from nineteen o six put its people at near two hundred ninety one thousand.

The isle runs one hundred fourteen miles long and fifty two miles wide. Forest clad mountains fill the greater part of its broad surface there. A main ridge curves from north west to south west across the isle. Side chains branch off and form small shut in basins all round. Mont Cinto, the top peak, rises to eight thousand eight hundred eighty one feet.
britannica-1911-credit-mobilier-of-ameri:
The Crédit Mobilier of America was a construction company tied to the building of the Union Pacific Railroad. Its work gave rise to a grave political scandal in the United States Congress. Chartered in 1859 as the Pennsylvania Fiscal Agency, it fell under Thomas Durant's control in March 1864. Durant, a vice-president of the Union Pacific, renamed it and used it as the road's building arm.

Government and mortgage bonds paid the company slightly more than the whole cost of construction. A congressional report put its extra gains in stock and bonds at 23,000,000 dollars, a profit of about 48 percent. In 1872 letters made public showed that Oakes Ames had placed shares with members of Congress. The House censured Ames and James Brooks in 1873. A Senate committee urged the expulsion of James W. Patterson, but his term expired before any action was taken.
britannica-1911-felucca:
Felucca is the name of a kind of boat in use on the inland sea, and a brief entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out its form. The word is Italian in its head form. Kin forms of it are found in Spanish and in French. It is most like of Arabic root, from words for a ship and for round in shape.

The craft is used for coast trade and for fish work. It is a long, low, and tight boat with no deck. It is built for speed in the main. Oars or sails drive it as the wind and the task call for. Its sails are of the lateen shape, the slant sail of that sea. They are borne on one or two masts set far to the front of the hull.
britannica-1911-foca:
Foca, pronounced Fawtcha, is a town of Bosnia set where the Drina and Cehotina rivers meet, ringed by wooded mountains. Its population in 1895 was 4,217. The town is headquarters of a thriving trade in silver filigree-work and inlaid weapons, for which it was famous. Its lands, enclosed by the frontiers of Montenegro and Novi Bazar, saw almost constant border warfare through the middle ages, when the town was known as Chocha.

No monuments of that age survive except the Bogomil cemeteries and the town's beautiful mosques, the oldest in Bosnia. Foca, Gorazda and Ustikolina were trading stations of the Ragusans in the fourteenth century. In the sixteenth century the Venetian ambassador Ramberti described it as Cozza, a large settlement of good Turkish-style houses, many shops and merchants. Through it all goods had to pass, and the governor of Herzegovina dwelt there.
britannica-1911-ghica:
Ghica is the name of a great Rumanian family in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its members played a large part in the making of modern Rumania. Many of them reigned as princes of Moldavia and Walachia. Rumanian historians give the family a humble start in Albania.

The founder, George Ghica, was by the tale a melon seller at Constantinople. A boyhood friend, risen to grand vizier, knew him in the street and raised him high. George became prince of Moldavia in 1658 and of Walachia the next year. He moved the Walachian capital from Tîrgovishtea to Bucharest for good. From him sprang the many branches of the house in both lands. He fostered a truly national Rumanian literature in its place. His brother Alexander ruled Walachia under a new organic statute.
britannica-1911-giordano-luca:
Luca Giordano, an Italian painter who lived from 1632 to 1705, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Naples, the son of Antonio, a poor painter who taught him the first steps of drawing. At the age of eight the boy painted a cherub into one of his father's pictures. The feat was talked of at once and won him a place under Ribera.

His father then took him to Rome to study under Pietro da Cortona. There he earned the nickname of Luca Fa-presto, Luke Work-fast. His father, poor and keen for gain, kept at him with the cry of Luca, work fast. The boy ate as he worked, fed by his father's hand. He copied the great works of Raphael and Michelangelo again and again. His speed won him the names of Thunderbolt and Proteus.
britannica-1911-gradisca:
Gradisca is a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes a town in Austria on the bank of a river. Most of its fewer than four thousand souls were Italians by speech. Silk spinning forms the chief trade of the town in its mills.

The entry traces the town through a string of lords and states. It first lay in a border mark, then passed to a church prince. Venice took it and walled it strong in the late middle ages. An emperor won it back by gift after a short hold. Its lands were made a county for a great house, then merged for good.
britannica-1911-heidelberg-south-africa:
Heidelberg is a town and district of the Transvaal. The Vaal river bounds the district on the south. It includes the south-eastern Witwatersrand gold-fields. The town stands 42 miles south-east of Johannesburg. Durban lies 441 miles away by rail. Its population in 1904 was 3,220, of whom 1,837 were white. The town was founded in 1865. It is built on the Rand's slopes at 5,029 feet.

That elevation gives it a strong health reputation. It is reputed the best sanatorium in the colony. The town is the centre of the eastern Rand gold mines. The entry is a brief gazetteer notice. Position, population and founding year are its facts. The gold-fields and the sanatorium claim complete it. No church, history or trade detail is added.
britannica-1911-huancavelica:
Huancavelica is a city of central Peru and capital of a department, 160 m. S.E. of Lima. It stands in a deep ravine of the Andes, at about 12,400 ft. above the sea, the ravine averaging a mile wide. Its people were put at 6,000 in 1906. The city is solidly and regularly built of stone, and stone bridges span the stream that runs through it.

Near the city lies the famous quicksilver mine of Santa Barbara. Its church of San Rosario is hewn underground from the native cinnabar-bearing rock. Viceroy Francisco de Toledo founded Huancavelica in 1572 as a mining town, and mining remains the chief occupation of its people. The department, crossed by the Cordillera Occidental, held 167,840 people in 1906 over 9,254 square miles. The short account closes with its products and climate.
britannica-1911-ica:
Ica, a city of southern Peru, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the capital of a department of the same name. The city lies one hundred and seventy miles south-east of Lima. A railway links it to its port, Pisco, on the Pacific coast.

Ica stands in a valley watered by its own river, in the foothills of the Andes. Irrigation makes that valley rich in vineyards and cotton fields. A desert strip parts the valley from the sea. The town was founded in 1563 and twice wrecked by earthquakes that century and the next. A Chilean raid in 1882 did it grave harm as well. Still it thrives on trade and industry, with a large cotton factory at its heart. Wine making ranks high in the valley, and much brandy goes out through Pisco. Fruit drying is noted as a new and growing trade.
britannica-1911-jaca:
Jaca is a city of northern Spain in the province of Huesca, among the south slopes of the Pyrenees. The 1911 Britannica article puts it 2,380 feet above the sea, on the left bank of the river Aragon. Its count in 1900 was 4,934. Jaca is the seat of a bishop and was once capital of the county of Sobrarbe. Its great Gothic cathedral dates at least from the eleventh century, and may be as old as the ninth.

The city draws weight from its post on the old frontier road from Saragossa to Pau. In 1904 France and Spain agreed to add a rail line from Oloron to Jaca. Forts were built near by at the close of the nineteenth century. The start of the city is unknown. Strabo names its tribe among the famed small peoples of the Ebro basin. The Moors held Jaca from the eighth century.
britannica-1911-lucca:
Lucca, an old town of Tuscany in Italy, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the capital of its province, north east of Pisa. Its people in 1901 numbered about forty three thousand in the town and seventy three thousand in the commune. The town stands low in the valley of the Serchio, facing a horizon of hills.

Its walls, pierced by four gates, were begun in 1504 and finished in 1645, and they long ranked among the most noted in Italy. They still stand, well kept and picturesque, with bastions planted with trees. The city looks well built and solid. Its chief attraction lies in its many churches, most of a marked basilican type in the Pisan manner. They show richly decorated fronts, fine apses and square bell towers. The cathedral of Saint Martin was begun in 1063 by Bishop Anselm, later Pope Alexander the Second.
britannica-1911-malacostraca:
Malacostraca is a title in zoology for a set of groups of crustacea. The groups are joined by marks that show a shared birth, the article says. Yet some, and most likely all, of them split apart in far past ages of the earth. Some have now reached a marked place apart from the rest. Since 1860, study of the set has added a great throng of new species, kinds, and families. It has also cast much light on hard points in their study.

Those points include their lines of birth, their place in the order of life, and their spread in the seas. They also include their build, their ways of life, and their worth to man. There are at least seven orders in the set. Four have stalked eyes, and three have eyes set flat in the head.
britannica-1911-middelburg-south-africa:
Middelburg is the subject of a town article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Middelburg is a town in the Transvaal in South Africa, east of Pretoria by rail. It stands on the high veld, over five thousand feet above the sea. A head stream of the Olifants River runs near it. By 1904 its people numbered just over five thousand.

The article calls it the chief town of a large district and a trading centre. It is also the centre of one of the richest coal fields in South Africa. Nearby mines yield fine steam coal, and copper and cobalt are found close by. In 1901 the town hosted peace talks between the British and the Boers. Lord Kitchener met General Botha there, but the talks failed after some weeks. The text also notes a second Middelburg in the Cape Province.
britannica-1911-modica:
Modica is a town in Sicily, in the province of Syracuse. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets it on a hill between two valleys. The church of Saint Giorgio crowns the hill on the old town site. That site was once the Sicel town called Motyca in old times.

The newer town spreads along the Mauro river below. A flood of that river did wide harm in September 1902. South east of town lies the Cava d Ispica valley. Its rock sides hold hundreds of cut grottoes. A few are Sicel tombs, but most are early Christian tombs or later cave homes.
britannica-1911-north-america:
North America is treated in this 1911 Britannica article by matching its land forms against those of the Old World. Set beside the northern lands of Eurasia, it shows a strong likeness, but with the parts reversed, right and left, like the two hands. The Laurentian highlands match Scandinavia and Finland, both untouched by folding since very ancient times.

A chain of waters marks the border of those old lands in both cases: the Great Lakes in America, and the southern Baltic with lakes Onega and Ladoga in Europe. The worn Appalachian mountains match the Hercynian ranges of middle Europe in their past. The central plains of North America match the plains of Russia and western Siberia. Both stretch from enclosed seas in the south to the Arctic Ocean in the north.
britannica-1911-paca:
Paca is a short 1911 Britannica article on a large rodent from Brazil. The paca is heavily built, short-tailed, and easy to spot by the light spots on its fur. Its Latin name is given as Coelogenys paca. The animal is kin to the agoutis and sits in the family Caviidae.

The text tells pacas apart from agoutis by their bulk and build. It notes their five-toed hind feet and their odd skull, where the cheek bones form large cases at the sides of the face. Their habits match those of agoutis, but when chased they always take to the water. The young stay in burrows for months, and the flesh is eaten in Brazil. A note on the paca-rana of Peru closes the piece.
britannica-1911-pinacotheca: Pinacotheca, a word for a picture gallery, is the subject of a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It comes from a Greek term built on the word for a tablet or picture. The name is best known for the picture wing of the Propylaea on the Acropolis at Athens. The Romans took the term for a room in a house that held pictures and statues.
britannica-1911-portuguese-east-africa:
Portuguese East Africa, also called Mozambique, is the subject of a regional entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry gives it an area of 293,500 square miles. The Indian Ocean bounds it on the east, and German East Africa on the north. Rhodesia, the Transvaal, and other lands lie to its west and south.

The Zambezi river cuts the land in two uneven parts. North of the river lies a compact block, about four hundred miles long. South of it the land is a coast strip, fifty to two hundred miles deep. The coast runs some 1,430 miles, with a double curve that trends east. Delagoa Bay cuts deep into the shore near the south border. Northward lie Sofala Bay, the wide delta of the Zambezi, and many small coral islands.
britannica-1911-sciacca:
Sciacca is a place article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a town and bishop's see on the south coast of Sicily. Sciacca stands in the province of Girgenti, 45 miles by road from that city, and held 24,645 people in 1906. Walls raised in 1400 ring it, and two ruined castles recall the Luna and Perollo families, whose feud ran from 1410 to 1529. The cathedral, founded in 1090, was much rebuilt in 1686, and fine medieval palaces and churches stand about the town.

Three miles east rises Monte San Calogero, the Mons Cronius of old, with sulphur and salt springs and vapour baths known to the Romans as the Thermae Selinuntiae. The name Sciacca is Arabic, though its meaning is unsure. The town also claims Tommaso Fazello, born there in 1498 and called the father of Sicilian history.
britannica-1911-sciatica: Sciatica is a form of nerve pain centred in the sciatic nerve and its roots. Its brief medical entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica gives the word roots in Latin and Greek terms for the hip joint. The entry classifies the condition under neuralgia and points readers to that fuller article for treatment and causes. No case history or remedy is given in this short notice itself, which serves as a definition and a cross reference only.
britannica-1911-sessa-aurunca:
Sessa Aurunca is a town and bishop's see in Campania, Italy, in the province of Caserta. It stands on the south-west slope of the dead volcano of Rocca Monfina, 666 feet above the sea. The town lies 27 miles by rail west-north-west of Caserta. Its people numbered 5,945 in the town and 22,077 in the wider commune. Sessa stands on the site of the old Suessa Aurunca, on a small stream that feeds the Liri.

The hill under Sessa is a mass of volcanic tufa. The town holds many old remains, such as a brick bridge of twenty-one arches. There are old bases under the church of S. Benedetto and a square stone building under a monastery. An old theatre also survives in part. The cathedral is a Romanesque basilica begun in 1103, with a mosaic floor, a fine pulpit on columns, and a Paschal candle stand.
britannica-1911-signorelli-luca:
Luca Signorelli, a Tuscan wall painter, opens a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Cortona about 1442, he took his art from that school. Perugia's masters first shaped his eye for form and hue. Kin ties sent him to learn under Piero della Francesca in youth. By 1472 he was at work at Arezzo with his own hand.

In 1474 Signorelli painted at Città di Castello in Umbria. A picture of Pan's school went from him to Lorenzo de Medici. Holy scenes by him show study of Botticelli and Lippi both. Pope Sixtus the Fourth set him to fresco work at Loreto. One fresco of his hand stands in the Sistine Chapel at Rome. It shows the acts of Moses in that famed room of art.
britannica-1911-south-america:
South America is treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica from its rocks upward. The entry opens on the continent's early physical history. Later events have largely wiped or hidden that record. The oldest land areas are guessed from today's granite and gneiss outcrops. The largest runs along the east coast, from the Plata toward the Amazon. Another old area lay over the highlands of Guiana.

A chain of islands once ran down the whole west side. On those old shores the seas laid down Cambrian beds. At the close of that period the land rose and islands joined. The continent grew much larger as a result. Silurian seas still covered the basin of the Paraguay, though. They ran from the Brazilian coast to the Andes axis. In Devonian times the land rose further. Islands merged and the old sea in the east basin vanished.
britannica-1911-ustica: Ustica is an island off the north coast of Sicily in this short 1911 Britannica place note. It lies north north west of Palermo. Its folk count fell to one thousand nine hundred sixteen in nineteen oh one. Greeks called the isle Osteodes, while Roman days knew it as Ustica. The whole isle is fire rock and shakes with quakes. Its soil is rich for crops. A large jail colony sits there. Roman tombs cut in the rock still show.
bundling-its-origin-progress-and-decline:
Henry Reed Stiles wrote a study of bundling, the old courtship custom, printed at Albany in 1871. A friend's sharp words set him to the work. Deacon Jabez H. Hayden had hit at a line on bundling in Stiles's History of Ancient Windsor. The hit, kind on both sides, drove a deep search of the point.

A Grant Thorburn line fronts the book: all writers agree, he says, that Yankees are a talking, guessing, swapping, and bundling folk. Start, spread, and fall of the custom form the book's three beats, as its title vows. Church, home, and court records of New England give the proof base. Stiles had form in town history — Brooklyn and Windsor both bear his name — and the same dig-and-cite hand runs this odd, small field. Shame, jest, and defence of New England's good name drive the pages.
burke-s-speech-on-conciliation-with-amer:
Burke's Speech on Conciliation with America presents Edmund Burke and his great parliamentary argument for settling with the American colonies, in an edition prepared for students by Sidney Carleton Newsom. Newsom, a teacher of English at Indianapolis, wrote the introduction for readers without a well stocked library, drawing on older editions and a bibliography he lists in full. The speech itself follows his framing chapters.

Contents pages lay out the study plan: the political situation, Burke as statesman, Burke in literature, topics for special reports, and then the speech with notes and an index. In the address, Burke urges Parliament to win the colonies back by concession rather than force, arguing from trade, distance, and the spirit of liberty in America. This printing serves the classroom: a classic piece of political persuasion, wrapped in the help a young reader needs to follow it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-africa:
Africa, a name of Phoenician origin, was first given by Romans to the territory around Carthage. It gradually spread to the whole Libyan territory Rome occupied. It was still understood in that sense in the eleventh century, when Leo IX wrote that after the Roman pontiff, Carthage's bishop stands first in Nubia and as Africa's chief metropolitan. Arabs then adopted the name, then medieval writers, until it came to cover the entire continent.

Africa spans about 12,000,000 square miles, about three times Europe and five times the United States without Alaska. It joins Asia only by the Suez Isthmus. Its shape is an irregular triangle, and its scarcity of bays and harbours seriously affected its history before steam. It rests on a rocky foundation forming an immense interior plateau, whence ranges like the Atlas branch off. The long entry moves from geography and peoples to missions and Islam.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agostino-cias:
Agostino Ciasca, in the world Pasquale, was an Italian Augustinian cardinal, born at Polignano a Mare, in Bari province, on 7 May 1835. He died at Rome on 6 February 1902. He took the Augustinian habit in 1856, made profession in 1857, and was ordained priest in 1858. Having perfected himself at Rome in philosophy, theology, and canon law, he devoted himself particularly to Oriental languages, especially Arabic and Coptic.

Exemplary in life and loyal to the church, he became dear to Leo XIII, who gave him confidence and entrusted him with several delicate missions. In his order he served as professor, prefect of studies, assistant general, and procurator general. Later he served at the Vatican Council as theologian and interpreter for Oriental bishops. His chief works include Coptic-Sahidic biblical fragments from the Borgia Museum and Tatian's Arabic gospel harmony, edited with a Latin translation in 1888.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alvar-nunez-c:
Alvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca, born at Jerez de la Frontera in Andalusia, has uncertain birth and death dates. His peasant family called themselves Alhaja until Las Navas de Tolosa, 1212. Turning the Arab position by a mountain pass, marked by a cow's skull, won them nobility. He joined Narváez's Florida expedition in 1526 as treasurer, one of four mainland survivors with two Spaniards and an Arab Moor.

Eight years roaming Louisiana and Texas coasts ended when his scant medicine and faith cures made him a renowned medicine man. After nine years they reached Sonora's Pacific coast, first Europeans across North America. He reached Mexico City in 1536, first European to see and describe the bison. La Plata governor from 1541, he was rebelled against in 1543, sent to Spain, and kept eight years in mild captivity. His Naufragios of 1542 and Comentarios of 1555 remain key sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrosian-bas:
The Ambrosian Basilica at Milan was raised by its great fourth-century bishop St. Ambrose and consecrated in the year 386. Its present form rose in four different periods, three in the ninth century and the fourth in the twelfth, though the original church is gone. Ambrose's own writings and modern research still give a fair idea of the founder's church. The original edifice resembled Rome's great churches of its age.

The basilica's story turns on Ambrose's final victory over the Arian court faction, after which the people sought its consecration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-america:
America, the Western Continent or New World, holds three main divisions. North America runs from about 70 to 15 degrees north, Central America's isthmus narrows to thirty miles at Panama, and South America from 12 degrees north to 55 south. Animism underlies the Indian creed everywhere, fetishism its tangible form, and monotheism, a personal all-creating ruling God, nowhere existed. Five European nations chiefly settled the continent after Columbus: Spain, Portugal, France, England, and Holland in date order; Sweden's small colony lasted under seventeen years.

Spanish exploration's precious-metal mines were worked progressively through the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, then faded. The peoples later fought through the Napoleonic period to secure independence. No sufficient data fix America's Catholic population; even the United States' usual 14,000,000 is a conjecture more or less accurate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angelo-rocca:
Angelo Rocca founded Rome's Angelica Library. Born at Rocca, now Arcevia, near Ancona, in 1545, he died at Rome on 8 April 1620. At seven he was received into the Augustinian monastery at Camerino, hence also called Camers or Camerinus, and he studied at Perugia, Rome, and Venice. Padua made him a doctor in theology in 1577.

In 1579 he became secretary to the Augustinian superior-general, in 1585 he took charge of the Vatican printing office, and he supervised the planned Bible and Fathers' editions. He became sacristan in the papal chapel in 1595, and in 1605 titular Bishop of Tagaste in Numidia. Rome's Augustinian public library, formally established on 23 October 1614, keeps his name. Mainly through his efforts came the Vulgate edition published under Clement VIII. He also edited Egidio Colonna and Augustinus Triumphus, and wrote on the sacraments, Scripture, canonization, and bells.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apiarius-of-s:
Apiarius, a priest of Sicca in Roman Africa, matters in history only because his appeal to Rome sparked a long dispute between Rome and Carthage over who controls church discipline. Deposed by Urbanus, bishop of Sicca, for serious misconduct, he appealed to Pope Zosimus, who found flaws in the bishop's procedure, ordered the priest restored, and had the bishop disciplined. A general synod at Carthage in May 418 then forbade clerics below bishop to appeal beyond the seas, meaning across the Mediterranean to Rome.

Opponents of the papacy later read African resentment in the case as a denial of papal supremacy, the doctrine of the pope's supreme authority. Apiarius became the classic example in anti-Roman controversy for a fifth-century rejection of papal control. The article presents the case as a disciplinary quarrel that grew into a lasting argument about African church freedom and Roman claims.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arca:
An arca was a box in which early Christians kept the Eucharist, the consecrated bread, in their homes. Cyprian tells of a woman who tried with unworthy hands to open her box holding the Lord's holy body. Fire issued from it the moment she touched it, and she could not open it. Wilpert believes a fresco in the catacomb of Saints Peter and Marcellinus shows such a box. It shows Christ seated reading from an open roll, three jars on his right, and on his left a square box filled with loaves, emblems of the Eucharist.

Arca also meant a receptacle for Christians' offerings for the church or the poor, cited from Tertullian and the Liber Pontificalis, the book of popes. The entry joins a devotional object and a charity chest under one Latin word, showing how early believers guarded the sacrament at home and gave for the common good.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-barca:
Barca was a titular see of Cyrenaica in northern Africa. Most archaeologists place it at Medinet el Merdja, though Graham puts it at Tolometa, or Tolmeita. Often destroyed and restored, it sank in the Roman period to a mere borough, yet still held a bishopric.

Its bishop Zopyros attended Nicaea in 325; Zephyrius is a mistaken form of his name. Zenobius and Theodorus appear in the subscriptions at Ephesus in 431 and Chalcedon in 451. Three bishops across three councils are all the record preserves. The see must have vanished when Arabs conquered the Pentapolis in 643.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartholomew-o:
Bartholomew of Braganca was born about 1200 and died on 1 July 1271. Studying at Padua, he received the Dominican habit from St Dominic himself. In 1248 he was appointed to the Cypriot see of Nemonicum, a city now unknown. In 1254 he was sent as legate to England and France, following Henry III to Paris. There France's king gave him a relic of the true Cross and a thorn from the Crown.

Alexander IV made him Bishop of Vicenza in 1256, where he endured the tyranny of Ezzelino, religion's notorious enemy. The persecution drew out his high pastoral qualities, and he built Vicenza's Dominican Church of the Crown to house his relics. He joined King Louis of France at Joppa, Sidon, and Acre during the crusading expedition. Venerated by the people and honored as Blessed, he also wrote scriptural commentaries and sermons.

Bartholomew of Lucca was a historian born at Lucca about 1227, who died about 1327. Entering the Dominicans young, he won St Thomas Aquinas's respect and friendship as disciple, confidant, and confessor. In 1272 he followed Thomas from Rome to Naples, learning of his master's death at Fossa Nuova in 1274. He became prior of his native convent in 1288 and of Santa Maria Novella at Florence in 1301.

At Avignon he served nine years as chaplain to cardinals, and John XXII made him Bishop of Torcello in 1318. A clash with Grado's patriarch over an abbess brought excommunication and exile in 1321, but peace returned him in 1323. His best-known Annales, covering 1061 to 1303 in terse sentences, was finished about 1307. He verified statements with care, though his age's uncritical temper let fables like Popess Joan stand.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartolommeo-p:
Bartolommeo Pacca was a cardinal, scholar, and statesman, born at Benevento in 1756, who died at Rome in 1844. Schooled by Jesuits at Naples and at Rome's Clementine College, he became nuncio at Cologne in 1785, a center of anti-Roman agitation. Consecrated titular Archbishop of Damiata, he arrived in June 1786 to find Cologne, Trier, and Mainz refusing recognition unless he renounced jurisdiction.

Other bishops and Cologne's magistrates received him respectfully, and even Prussia made no difficulty. Frederick William honored him on the Rhine, and Rome accorded the Prussian monarch the royal title. His Cologne position stayed difficult, as Bonn's new university preached open war on the Holy See. His memoirs record acute observations on politics and history, including his Cologne nunciature and the years 1809 to 1814.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-basilica:
Basilica is a word with two senses: a church's architectural style and its canonical status. In architecture it signifies a kingly, and secondarily beautiful, hall of Eastern origin, finest in Rome. Rome's Forum held basilicas of Porcia, Fulvia, Sempronia, and Opimia between 184 and 121 BC, then Caesar's Basilica Julia after 46 BC. They beautified the Forum and served markets and justice, open to the public and well lighted.

Vitruvius gives the usual plan: a parallelogram whose width runs between a third and a half of its length. Columns divide the middle space from a lower ambulatory as wide as the columns are high, with shorter upper columns admitting light. Canonically, basilica rank brings precedence over other churches, save the local cathedral, plus the conopaeum, bell, and cappa magna. The conopaeum, a red and yellow silk umbrella, is carried with the bell at the clergy's head on state occasions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cardica:
Cardica was a titular see of Thessaly, the Latinized medieval form of Gardicium, truly Gardikion in Greek. It appears only in later see-lists from the 1100s or 1200s, under Larissa. Lequien names five Latin bishops from 1208 to 1389, beginning with Bartholomew, recipient of many letters from Pope Innocent III.

Lequien knew no Greek bishop of the see, but manuscript lists add eight names. They run from John in 1191 to Gregorius about 1852, with Metrophanes degraded in 1623 and Sophronius serving from 1646 to 1649. When Thessaly joined Greece in 1881 the see had stood vacant since 1875. It was suppressed in 1899, and Gardiki survives as a small town of about 3,000 people in the diocese of Phthiotis.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholic-knig:
The Catholic Knights of America was a fraternal life-insurance company chartered under Kentucky law. Four Nashville men founded it. James J. McLoughlin led the group. D. N. Burke joined him, as did John Broderick and John McDonald. They first met on 23 April 1877 at Emmett Hall. The society began as the Order of United Catholics and later took its new name at Bishop P. A. Feehan's suggestion. Feehan, of Nashville, became its spiritual director.

Growth was rapid: sixteen branches met in the first supreme council at Louisville in July 1878, and seventy-two were represented at Indianapolis the next year. By 1 August 1907 the order counted 20,000 members in 560 branches across forty-two states. It had paid nearly fifteen million dollars to heirs of over 8,500 deceased members, and held resources of $828,000.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholic-univ:
The Catholic University of America is a pontifical institution in Washington, D.C., comprising schools of Sacred Sciences, Philosophy, Law, Letters, and Science. Supreme authority rests with the Holy See, while governing power lies with the bishops of the United States, exercised through a board of trustees of bishops, priests, and laymen. The Archbishop of Baltimore serves as chancellor ex officio, and a rector, aided by an academic senate, runs the university day to day.

The desire for such a university was voiced at the Second Plenary Council of Baltimore in 1866 and took definite shape at the Third in 1884. By 1907 the university counted 32 teachers and 210 students, with a library of 100,000 volumes and its own quarterly, The Catholic University Bulletin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clerks-regula:
The Clerks Regular of the Mother of God of Lucca were founded by Blessed Giovanni Leonardi, born in 1541 at Diecimo in the Republic of Lucca. Sent to Lucca at seventeen to learn the apothecary's trade, he was piously inclined from childhood and was ordained on 22 December 1572. His congregation began in 1574, when two or three young laymen gathered round him for guidance in reforming manners and saving souls.

When his lay helpers prepared for priesthood and a religious order took shape, persecution broke out. The Fathers of the republic feared a native order spreading over Italy would expose the little state's affairs. Persecution kept Leonardi mostly banished from Lucca, admitted only by special Senate decree under papal pressure. In 1580 he secretly acquired Santa Maria Cortelandini, still held by his sons. Bishop Guidiccioni canonically erected the congregation in 1583 at Gregory the Thirteenth's instigation, confirmed by Clement the Eighth's brief of 13 October 1595.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-concordia-in-:
Adolphus Ennis's entry covers the Diocese of Concordia in northwestern Kansas. Erected on 2 August 1887, it borders Colorado west, Nebraska north, and county lines east and south, across 26,685 square miles. In 1886 Leavenworth split into three sees: Leavenworth, Wichita, and Concordia. Richard Scannell of Nashville, nominated first bishop on 9 August 1887, ruled until 30 January 1891, when he moved to Omaha. Wichita's bishop then administered Concordia, and no new bishop came until 1897.

Growth followed fast. From 1898 to 1907, forty-five churches and twenty schools rose, besides new missions and stations. An 1884 boarding school for young ladies under the Sisters of Saint Joseph had led the way. By the time of writing, fifty-one secular and fifteen religious priests served ninety-one churches, thirty stations, and four chapels. Parochial schools held about 2,482 children, and academies at Concordia and Abilene about 135 pupils. The Catholic population stood at 26,125.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-corsica:
Alexandre Guasco's entry covers Corsica, the Mediterranean's third island in size, surpassed only by Sicily and Sardinia. Antibes on the French Riviera lies one hundred and eleven miles from Calvi, Corsica's port nearest France. Brisk commerce runs between Leghorn in Italy and Bastia in Corsica, the voyage taking five hours. The island is mountainous and well watered, largely covered with forests and almost impenetrable thickets called maquis.

Coastal climate stays mild, while elevated regions run cold. Corsica's area measures 3,367 square miles, its population 300,000. Interior and coastal natives alike, descended from Italians, are nearly all Catholics. Phoenicians and Phocians early visited the island and established colonies there. For a time it belonged to Carthage. Christianity, it has been asserted, entered Corsica in Apostolic times. Before and after 600 the island stood in close dependence on the Apostolic See, and always remained so.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-of-sa:
The Council of Sardica, held most probably in 343, belongs to the series of councils wrestling with Arian doctrine and its fallout. Emperors Constans and Constantius convoked it at Pope Julius's urging, choosing Sardica, now Sofia, for a genuinely representative meeting. Athanasius and other bishops, condemned and vindicated by turns, awaited a final judgment.

Eastern bishops, in the minority, withdrew to act as a body, while the remainder refused to add to the Nicene Creed and enacted canons on bishops' transfers, trials, and appeals. Documents went to Pope Julius with a majority letter, yet pacification failed entirely, and the Eastern bishops grew bolder in defiance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cuenca:
A diocesan entry describes Cuenca, a suffragan see of Quito in Ecuador, created in 1779. Its episcopal city, 7,700 feet above sea level in a broad plain south-east of Guayaquil, holds 30,000 people, with Peruvian antiquities nearby. The diocese covers Azuay and Canar, and ranks second among Ecuadorian sees.

Jesuits led the first missions, followed by Franciscans, Dominicans, and others, working 130 successful years until the Society's expulsion in 1767. A Salesian mission now works eastward in Gualaquiza. The Franciscan Vicente Solano, famed as a controversialist, belonged to this diocese. Its organization owes most to Bishop Toral, who served from 1861 to 1883 and attended the Vatican Council.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cuernavaca:
A church entry covers Cuernavaca, set up in 1891 for the whole state of Morelos in Mexico. It is bounded by the archdioceses of Mexico and Puebla and the bishopric of Chilapa. It spans 7,184 square kilometres with 161,697 people, served in 34 parishes by 42 diocesan and 6 order priests.

Franciscans first preached the Gospel here, founding the Cuernavaca convent in 1526. Dominicans followed at Oaxtepec in 1529, and Augustinians at Ocuituco in 1534. By 1536, the Franciscan writer Motolinia claims, all the people had turned to the Faith. In the 1700s most churches passed from the orders to diocesan clergy. The first bishop, Fortino Hipolito Vera, was consecrated in 1894 and died four years later.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dacca:
A diocesan entry traces Dacca, a see in Bengal, India, from Portuguese jurisdiction to its own hierarchy. By a constitution of Paul III in 1534, Goa held spiritual rule from the Cape of Good Hope as far as China. Bengal's early Portuguese settlements fell under Goa. From 1606 they fell under Mylapore.

When British rule replaced Portugal, Mylapore still kept jurisdiction, and 7,000 of Dacca's 22,000 Catholics remained subject to it. For effective mission work, Propaganda made a Jesuit vicar apostolic of Calcutta and Bengal in 1834. Pius IX divided Bengal into two vicariates in 1850. A third followed in 1870. On the creation of the Indian hierarchy in 1886, the eastern vicariate rose to the Diocese of Dacca.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diego-alvarez:
Diego Alvarez Chanca served as court physician to the Spanish sovereigns Ferdinand and Isabella. He sailed with Christopher Columbus on his second voyage to America in 1493. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry credits him with treating Columbus through a bout of malarial fever soon after landing in Haiti. He also saved other leaders of the expedition who fell sick.

On ground Chanca himself chose, the settlers raised Isabella, the first Christian town in the New World. It was named for the queen. His letter to the council of his home city, written after only three months on shore, stands as the first account of American plants, animals, and peoples.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-domenico-capr:
Domenico Capranica was a cardinal, theologian, canonist, and statesman, born near Palestrina in 1400. At Padua and Bologna he studied canon and civil law brilliantly, winning the doctorate of both laws at twenty-one. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows him as secretary to Martin the Fifth and apostolic prothonotary, made cardinal in secret in 1423 or 1426, though his rank was not proclaimed until 1430.

He earned swift rise by political and military service, ruling Imola and Forli and winning back rebellious Bologna. He became bishop of Fermo and played a part at the Council of Basle, of which he is said to have written a history never printed. His Rules of Life for a nephew, the entry notes, mirror a fine character. He died at Rome in 1458.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fabriano-and-:
Fabriano and Matelica form one diocese in central Italy, in the province of Macerata. Fabriano is famed for paper works and salted-fish trade. It is said to descend from refugees of ancient Attidium in the ninth century before Christ. Its baptismal font stayed at Attigio until 1254. Its story runs with the Marches.

San Benedetto holds the tomb of Blessed Giovanni Bonnelli, dead in 1290. Saint Silvestro Guzzoli, founder of that order, lies at Monte Fano nearby, and the relics of Saint Romuald moved to Saints Biagio and Romoaldo in 1480. Fabriano stood under Camerino until 1785, when Pius VI restored Matelica and joined it to Fabriano as equal heads. Matelica was a Roman colony from 89 before Christ, and its ancient bishops Equitius and Florentius are named. Gentile da Fabriano, the painter, was its most famed native.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-german-roman-:
The German Roman Catholic Central Verein of North America united German Catholic benevolent societies against secret societies and for Catholic rights. Its origin lies in 1854, when presidents of three Buffalo societies called German Catholic bodies together, urged by missionary priests and approved by Bishop Timon. A Mainz union of 1848 lent the model, and seventeen societies organized the Verein at Baltimore's Saint Alphonsus Hall on April 15, 1855.

Membership stayed limited to German-language Catholic benevolent societies, growing from seventeen societies and 1,500 members in 1855 to 548 societies and 48,989 members in 1895. A 1901 reorganization replaced direct local affiliation with state associations, and by 1907 sixteen state bodies and fifty-two locals counted 99,291 paid-up members. Pius IX praised the Verein in 1866, its fifty-two years gave about twelve thousand dollars to Peter's Pence, and its immigrant agents and Leo House in New York served newcomers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gioacchino-ve:
Gioacchino Ventura di Raulica was an Italian pulpit orator, patriot, and philosopher born at Palermo in 1792, who died at Versailles in 1861. He entered the Jesuits in 1808 and, when the order was suppressed in Sicily, joined the Theatines in 1817. Leo XII made him professor of canon law at the Sapienza, and in 1830 he became Superior-General of the Theatines. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows his preaching and his politics in turn.

His eloquence, vehement and direct with a magnificent voice, won him renown in Rome and Paris, where he almost rivaled Lacordaire. Under Pius IX he glorified the union of religion and liberty. He defended the Sicilian Revolution, dreaming of an Italian confederation under the pope. After the Roman Republic fell in 1849 he withdrew to France, preached before Napoleon III, and closed his life as a moderate Traditionalist philosopher.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-batt:
Giovanni Battista de Luca was a cardinal and Italian canonist of the seventeenth century, born at Venosa in southern Italy in 1614, who died at Rome in 1683. Born of humble parents, he studied at Naples, returned home in ill health, and went to Rome in 1645. There his legal skill won him a high reputation, along with much envy.
